0.description: Solar flares scour Tibedied's upper atmosphere on a schedule no almanac has ever fixed, and the fief-holds have learned to build low, thick-walled, and close together rather than trust the sky. Its industry is old and undercapitalised, more workshop than factory, turning out goods that serve the estates rather than any wider market. What fame the world holds comes from the vineyard terraces of the sheltered lowlands, where the grapes that go into Tibediedian Vees brandy are harvested in the brief calm windows between storms. The distilleries themselves are windowless stone cellars, built that way long before anyone understood why it mattered.
0.inhabitants: The native lobster-kind are placid, slow to anger, and organized under a lattice of hereditary holdings that has outlasted every attempt at reform. Labor is bound to the land and to the lord who holds it, and the comfortable living most families enjoy owes more to the brandy trade than to the industry that employs them. Generations of sheltering from the flares have made them a patient, indoor people, unhurried in speech and firm in custom.”}

1.description: Qube's landmass is dominated by great dense forests, broken only by the cleared belts where the grain and orchard estates run in careful geometric plots. The corporate charter that governs the world has organized much of the arable land into holdings tied directly to processing depots and rail spurs, and the timber margins have become the front lines of a civil war that has burned through several harvests. Settlements sit close to the forest edge, palisaded and watchful, and the smoke of contested tracts is often visible above the canopy. Despite the fighting, the agricultural output continues largely uninterrupted in the estates furthest from the fighting.
1.inhabitants: The population lives under the authority of the chartered companies that own the land they work, their loyalties often split between rival boards as much as between causes. Farmers, foresters and militia recruited from the same villages find themselves on opposing sides of the same access roads, and a wary, practical endurance has replaced any expectation that the fighting will end soon.

2.description: Leleer is a small world whose modest land area is given over almost entirely to industrial works and, along its warmer belts, the pink tulip plantations for which it is noted throughout the region. The Gesoaren fields are worked in long terraces below the smoke of processing plants, an arrangement that has done little for the health of the soil or the workers tending it. A disease of uncertain origin has spread through the settlements in recent years, resisting the world's developed medical infrastructure and leaving entire districts under quarantine.
2.inhabitants: The population, dense for so small a world, lives under a dictatorship that directs labour toward the plantations and factories with equal firmness, tolerating little disruption to output. Comfortable wealth is spread unevenly, favouring those attached to the tulip trade or its refineries, while the sick and the quarantined make do with less. Colonials here are known for a grim practicality, having learned to keep working through outbreaks that would halt production elsewhere.

3.description: Biarge presents a skyline of competing corporate and civic enclaves, each answering to a different administration, stitched together across a landmass given over almost entirely to manufacturing and refinement. Smoke-scrubbed towers and pressurized foundries dominate the horizon, feeding an export economy built on high-grade goods rather than raw ore. The world's oddest renown lies in the cultivation of the Biargian edible poet, a delicacy bred and marketed with the same industrial precision applied to everything else here. Wealth is evident in the polish of its transit ways and the density of its housing blocks, though the divided governance keeps every district fiercely proprietary about its own patch of prosperity.
3.inhabitants: The population, fierce black bony humanoids, split their loyalties among the many overlapping authorities that govern Biarge, and this fractured rule has bred a people who negotiate as readily as they work. Labour is prized and status follows productivity, so households compete openly for contracts, patents, and the right to claim the finest strains of the famous poet as their own.

4.description: Xequerin's small crust is broken by volcanic vents that behave unlike those charted elsewhere, venting in slow rhythmic pulses rather than in continuous flow, and the ash from them feeds thin but productive foundries strung along the rift lines. Settlement clusters near these fissures, where geothermal heat drives the state's smelters and refineries. In the cooler upland reaches, the mountain lobstoid burrows through mineral-rich scree, an animal as strange to outsiders as the volcanoes it shares its slopes with.
4.inhabitants: The Large Frogs of Xequerin organize their labor communally, rotating between the foundry collectives and the lobstoid harvest camps according to season and directive. Their manner is unhurried but disciplined, shaped by a state that prizes steady output over individual gain, and by a comfortable, if modest, standard of living earned collectively rather than traded for.

5.description: Tiraor's surface is given over almost entirely to heavy manufacture, with refineries and foundries packed so close that their runoff has fouled the rivers and blackened the lower atmosphere for generations. The state has never prioritized cleanup over output, and successive production quotas have left slag heaps, chemical ponds and smog banks as permanent features of the landscape. Its reputation as a foul, corroded world is earned rather than exaggerated, yet the factories continue to run at full capacity and the planet remains one of the wealthier producers in its region.
5.inhabitants: Labor is organized through party-run collectives that assign housing, food and work with little regard for individual preference, producing a population accustomed to discipline and shared hardship. Generations spent in the mills and chemical plants have bred a stoic, practical outlook, and most residents take a grim pride in output figures rather than in the condition of the world that generates them.

6.description: Rabedira's continents are stitched together by rail lines and refinery stacks that mark it as an average industrial world, its skies hazed by the output of foundries scattered across competing territories. The planet's many governments have fought each other to ruin more than once, and swathes of the equatorial belt still show the blackened frames of settlements burned in the last civil war. Amid the wreckage its people cling with peculiar fierceness to a shared cultural loathing of sit coms, a rare point of agreement among factions that otherwise trust nothing from beyond their own borders.
6.inhabitants: The population lives divided among rival administrations, each running its own courts, currency controls and industrial quotas, yet the comfortable wealth spread through the working districts keeps outright want at bay. Generations of factional conflict have made the colonials guarded and practical, quick to rebuild after every ceasefire and quicker still to distrust any single authority claiming to speak for the whole world.

7.description: Lave's surface is dominated by dense rain forest, broken only by scattered clearings where the colonial farms cut their fields from the canopy. The Lavian tree grub, harvested from the deep forest and prized off-world as a delicacy, remains the world's best-known export and the one thing most travellers have heard of before they hear anything else about it. Farming here is done largely by hand and beast, the tools and methods of the settlers little advanced from the days of first landing.
7.inhabitants: The colonials live thinly spread through the forest edge, working small holdings and grub-camps under a dictatorship that leaves the daily business of farming to itself so long as tribute and order are kept. Life is modest and unhurried by necessity rather than choice, shaped by primitive tools, poor roads, and a government more interested in control than improvement.

8.description: Zaatxe's continents are given over almost entirely to refineries, foundries and the close-packed housing blocks that serve them, the whole surface organised under charter by the corporate boards that own it outright. The world is wealthy by any measure, its wealth built on heavy manufacture rather than trade, and its cities run in shifts around the clock to keep the furnaces fed. It is mildly noted among naturalists for the Zaatxian Isdimaoid, a venomous native species now confined to the shrinking wild margins, but the planet's more pressing distinction is the plague of lethal yaks that has overrun outlying farmland and idle industrial ground alike, resisting every corporate effort at eradication.
8.inhabitants: The Fierce Fat Birds who populate Zaatxe are organised less as citizens than as shareholders and shift-workers, their lives structured tightly around company hierarchy and production quotas. Generations spent in the service of the boards have left them blunt, proprietary about their work, and openly contemptuous of the yaks that harass their perimeter fences and eat into every quarter's output.

9.description: Diusreza is a large world of modest industry, its factories scattered thin across broad continents under the control of feudal holdings rather than any central authority. The planet's moths are notorious: prized as a delicacy across every household table, yet capable of killing the unwary who mishandle or undercook them. Despite this hazard, or perhaps because of it, the local holdings have built a curious reputation for welcoming outsiders with open enthusiasm, treating every visit as occasion for feasting and spectacle.
9.inhabitants: The Horned Lobsters who hold Diusreza's fiefs divide their labour between the poor foundries that keep the world modestly industrial and the moth harvests that sustain both diet and legend. Feudal lords compete for status not through wealth, which remains thin across the population, but through the lavishness of their hospitality toward strangers, a trait that has become something of a local obsession. Ordinary folk get by on modest means, wary of the moths they cannot stop eating and proud of a fame built on danger they treat as festivity.

10.description: Teaatis is a large world of scattered holdings, its distances too great and its roads too few to bind the land into anything more than a patchwork of manors and fields. Grain and root crops dominate the low country, tended by hand and ox under a primitive order that has changed little across generations. The world's chief renown lies in its vicious brew, a fermented spirit distilled in barns and cellars and traded between estates more readily than any crop. Settlements are few and far between, each little more than a manor house, its outbuildings, and the tenant plots that surround it.
10.inhabitants: The population lives bound to the land and to the lords who hold it, working fields and stills in roughly equal measure. Poverty is common and travel between holdings rare, so loyalty and grievance alike tend to stay local, passed down within a manor rather than across the world. What reputation Teaatis has beyond its own soil rests almost entirely on the brew its people distill and are known to drink strong and often.

11.description: Riinus turns beneath a canopy of rain forest that circles most of its equatorial belt, broken only by the terraced industrial districts carved into its highland margins. The canopy yields the Riinusian tree grub, harvested by cooperative gangs and processed in state-run canneries that ship the delicacy off-world under strict quota. Factory towns sit at the forest edge on raised concrete platforms, connected by rail lines that cut straight through the green rather than around it, and the constant runoff from the wet season keeps the lowland mills running on hydro power year-round.
11.inhabitants: The Black Fat Felines who work the grub harvests and assembly lines answer to district production committees rather than private owners, and pride in meeting or exceeding the forest quota runs deep in their culture. Wealth here is broadly shared but closely accounted, and even senior cadre are expected to have spent time knee-deep in canopy mud before moving to the ministries that plan the next season's harvest.

12.description: Esbiza's continents are dominated by rain forest canopy that runs unbroken from the equatorial belt into the temperate zones, broken only where industrial concessions have cut clearings for refineries and processing plants. The world's wealth comes from what is drawn out of that canopy and the ground beneath it, refined in complexes that sit like islands amid the green. Because no single authority governs the whole surface, jurisdictions overlap along old concession boundaries, each with its own tariffs, permits and enforcement, so a refinery district may answer to different rules than the forest tract supplying it.
12.inhabitants: Colonial families here tend to work within one concession for generations, moving between forest extraction crews and the processing towns that depend on them. The patchwork of authorities has made most residents fluent in negotiating rules that change at a district line, and comfortable wages have bought a settled, unhurried confidence rather than any urgency to leave.

13.description: Ontimaxe is a large world given over almost entirely to cultivation, its lowlands divided into a patchwork of grain and orchard holdings that stretch beyond the horizon in most directions. The climate is temperate and forgiving, and the modest technology available to farmers here is applied with care rather than force, producing steady yields without much waste. Kitchens across the settlements are unusually well equipped for a world of this technological standing, a fact locals attribute to a long-standing regional obsession with blending fruit, grain and dairy into every conceivable form. Market towns hold seasonal fairs centered on nothing but blender demonstrations, recipe contests and the trading of custom blades and jars.
13.inhabitants: The population lives comfortably on the proceeds of its harvests, and the democratic institutions here tend toward small elected boards that manage irrigation, storage and distribution with practical, unhurried debate. People take considerable pride in home cooking and in the machines that make it possible, treating a well-kept blender as something between a tool and an heirloom.

14.description: Cebetela's industry clusters in the lowland basins, refineries and distilleries feeding off ore veins and the fermented orchards that ring each settlement. The brandy distilled here, potent enough to be traded under warning labels elsewhere, is boiled and bottled in works towns strung along the foothills. Above them, the mountain ranges are the domain of the Laensooids, predators whose raids on outlying works have shaped where and how the settlements are built. With no central authority to coordinate defense or industry, each town operates as its own fortified concern, wary of the slopes at its back.
14.inhabitants: Cebetela's colonials are workers first, distillers and smiths who keep their machinery running with little outside help and less oversight. Lacking any government to organize defense, they arm their own perimeters against the mountain predators, and this constant vigilance has bred a population that trusts its neighbors in the works and almost no one beyond the fence line.

15.description: Ceedra's farmland stretches across temperate lowlands in broad, irregular parcels, the legacy of a confederacy that never quite managed to standardise its land grants. Grain silos and processing towns dot the countryside, many now scarred or abandoned where the civil war has passed through. The fighting moves in cycles across the agricultural belts, and settlements rebuild between offensives with a persistence that outsiders find hard to square with the disorder around them. Despite the damage, the world remains a comfortable and populous one, its silos generally fuller than its garrisons.
15.inhabitants: The lizards of Ceedra are famous well beyond their own system for a strain of silliness that persists even amid the civil war, trading jokes and elaborate nonsense rituals between skirmishes with a straight face that visitors rarely expect. Confederate loyalties run deep but overlap badly, and most disputes are settled with as much theatrical absurdity as actual violence, though the war itself is real and costly. Farmers, militia, and local assemblies alike seem equally capable of grim resolve and complete foolishness, often within the same conversation.

16.description: Rizala's broad continents are given over almost entirely to grain and orchard, with distilleries rising among the fields wherever the harvest outpaces the granaries. Settlements spread low and wide across the plains, linked by rail lines that exist mainly to move produce and drink between them rather than to concentrate industry in any one place. The confederated districts each claim their own vintage of the local brandy, a spirit strong enough that its reputation has spread well beyond the system despite nobody bothering to promote it. Fertile soil and a temperate, well-watered climate have made the world's size an asset rather than a burden, since nearly all of it can be farmed.
16.inhabitants: The Black Rodents who work Rizala's land are organized into semi-autonomous districts that bargain and vote through the confederacy rather than defer to any central authority, which suits a population more loyal to its home valley than to the world as a whole. Comfortable harvests and steady trade have left most households with more leisure than ambition, and a great deal of that leisure is spent arguing, amiably, over whose brandy is the more lethal.

17.description: Atriso's compact landmass is given over almost entirely to terraced farms and shallow aquaculture pans that ring its coastlines, feeding a population packed into dense agricultural townships. The world's reputation rests on kitchens that turn its odd, richly flavored crops and shellfish into dishes prized well beyond the system, served in market halls built more for spectacle than comfort. Rule here is absolute and centralized, with produce quotas and export licenses set from a single capital that treats the harvest as a matter of state.
17.inhabitants: The Horned Lobsters who work Atriso's fields and pans are known throughout for a cheerful, almost theatrical silliness that seems to survive every tightening of quota and decree. Life under the dictatorship is regimented and modest rather than comfortable, and most households get by on steady labor rather than surplus. Even so, festivals, puns, and elaborate food rituals thread through daily work, as if the planet's people have decided that dignity is optional but flavor is not.

18.description: Teanrebi's continents sit on restless plates, and the tremors that follow are frequent enough to shape every aspect of building and farming here. Fields are laid out in narrow terraces that can be replanted quickly after a shake collapses an irrigation channel or buries a paddock in silt. Settlements favour low, squat construction spread wide across the plains rather than tall structures, and the corporate charter that administers the world has invested more in early-warning towers than in grand architecture. Despite the size of the land under cultivation, the soil is thin and the harvests modest, leaving the world dependent on subsistence-level farming rather than surplus.
18.inhabitants: The bug-eyed frogs who work the land are organized under a single controlling company that leases plots, seed and tools in exchange for a share of every harvest, leaving most families with just enough to get by. Generations of sudden ground movement have made them quick to abandon a structure and slow to trust a still morning, and their folk wisdom is full of signs read from animal behaviour and shifting water tables. Communities cooperate readily in the aftermath of a quake, since rebuilding is a shared and constant labour rather than an occasional one.

19.description: Azaqu's oceans run a deep rose-pink, tinted by mineral algae blooms that stretch from horizon to horizon and give the coastal farmlands their characteristic ruddy soil. Grain and orchard estates spread across the lowlands, feeding a population spread thin across a world large enough that its regional assemblies rarely agree on much beyond trade tariffs. In the low-gravity habitats ringing the equatorial highlands, Zero-G cricket draws crowds from every province, played in vast tethered domes where the ball can travel for what feels like whole minutes before gravity reasserts itself.
19.inhabitants: Azaquans are farmers and administrators in roughly equal measure, used to settling disputes over water rights and grain quotas through endless committee votes rather than decree. Life here is unhurried and reasonably secure, and much civic pride rests on provincial cricket leagues, whose championships draw larger turnouts than most elections.

20.description: Retila spreads across a broad landmass of worn industrial belts and cratered flatlands, its skies prone to sudden storms of charged particles that sweep down from its sun. Smelters and refineries stand in clusters shielded by earthworks and scavenged plating, built up wherever the local warlords or cooperatives have managed to keep the lights on. Solar flares periodically knock out power grids and scorch exposed circuitry across whole districts, and the scars of these events are visible in the blackened frames of abandoned factories. What industry survives is patched together from older, sturdier equipment built to withstand the world's temperament.
20.inhabitants: Without any central authority, the population has organized into shifting factions and work-gangs that control production district by district, trading favors and materials more often than currency. Life here rewards those who can repair a generator blind and rebuild after a flare has passed, and most people carry that practical toughness in how they speak and work. Getting by is the common condition, and there is little pretense that it will change soon.

21.description: Sotiqu's farmland lies patched between scrubland and quarantine markers, worked in narrow plots by families who no longer trust their neighbors' water. The soup made from its hardy goat herds is prized off-world for a flavor found nowhere else, a reputation the planet clings to even as the disease that stalks its villages goes untreated. Settlements are few, spread thin across the plains, each one walled off more by fear than by fence. No central authority coordinates relief, quarantine, or trade, so the sickness spreads at whatever pace the land and its people allow.
21.inhabitants: The Fierce Frogs who hold this world answer to no government beyond the clan and the herd, and they guard both with a wariness bordering on hostility toward outsiders and each other alike. Generations of primitive tools and poor harvests have made them resourceful but suspicious, quick to defend a goat pen or a sickbed with equal violence. What trade they permit is conducted warily, soup and hides offered at a careful distance from strangers who might carry the next outbreak.

22.description: Inleus is a large world whose industrial belts ring low continents beneath a haze of manufacturing exhaust, its factories aging and its output modest against the wealth that flows through its banks and exchanges. Away from the mills, wide temperate reserves of scrub and forest remain protected by law, and it is there that the Inleusian spotted wolf still hunts, the animal for which the world is chiefly known offworld. Settlement is dense and continuous across the lowlands, tiers of housing built up around the old plants rather than replacing them.
22.inhabitants: The population is composed of small, slime-coated rodents, harmless and easily startled, who nonetheless run every layer of the democracy with the same patient committee-work applied to the wolf reserves. Wealth here sits apart from the industry that first built the world, so most work is now administrative, regulatory, or given over to the upkeep of the wilderness the wolf requires.

23.description: Onrira's atmosphere carries a permanent haze of ionised particles, the visible signature of a sun given to violent, unpredictable flares that periodically scour the outer settlements and disrupt surface power grids. Industry here has adapted around the problem: factories and refineries are built low, shielded, and clustered in deep valleys or beneath ridgelines away from open sky. The world's synthetic compound sold abroad as Xeoid, prized and feared in equal measure for its lethality, is manufactured in these shielded works, and the export trade has done much to fund Onrira's dense urban sprawl. Corporate towers dominate the skyline of every major city, their lower floors windowless against radiation surges.
23.inhabitants: Most residents work directly or indirectly for the handful of conglomerates that own the planet's mines, refineries and Xeoid production lines, and company loyalty runs deep, reinforced by generous wages and constant reminders of the alternative. Life is organised around flare warnings and shelter drills as much as shift schedules, giving the population a practical, unsentimental attitude toward risk. Wealth is visible but unevenly distributed, concentrated among executives and senior technicians who oversee the world's more hazardous work.

24.description: Ceinzala's farmland spreads across broad temperate belts, feeding processing towns that exist mainly to press and ferment the estate crop into Esti juice, a drink famed across the region for its bite. The world's fortune is shadowed by its star, whose flares and unpredictable outbursts disrupt communications, spoil harvests without warning, and force growers to plan around blackout seasons rather than calendars. Settlements are dense and close-packed, built low against the periodic radiation warnings, with cellars and shielded granaries doing double duty as storm shelters. Swarms of fierce-looking insects move through the fields, harmless to people but relentless against crop pests, and are tolerated as part of the agricultural order.
24.inhabitants: Life under a single ruling authority has organized the population into disciplined agricultural cooperatives, their routines built around the erratic temper of the sun as much as around planting seasons. Comfortable but never idle, they carry a reputation for stoic patience, riding out blackouts and crop scares with the same flat calm they bring to producing their notorious Esti juice.

25.description: Biisza's landmass lies mostly under continuous canopy, its rain forests broken only by river deltas and the cleared terraces where the colony grows its staple crops. Settlements follow the rivers rather than any planned grid, strung along the waterways that serve as the main routes between the clearings. The confederacy's member districts each hold a share of forest and farmland, and boundaries between them are marked as often by treaty as by any visible line on the ground.
25.inhabitants: Human Colonials here work the terraces and river trade that the forest allows, living comfortably without great surplus. Authority is shared among the confederated districts, so disputes over land and water rights are settled by council rather than decree, and people tend to speak of their district before they speak of the planet.

26.description: Legees is a small world of rich lowland soils and orchard belts, worked into terraces and irrigated fields that ring its scattered towns. The ground beneath these towns shifts often, and cracked foundations, propped-up granaries and rebuilt market walls are common sights across the farm districts. What draws outside notice is what happens after dusk, when the settlements light their squares and open the venues, dens and open-air gardens that give the planet its reputation for exotic night life. Between the tremors and the harvest cycles, life on Legees runs to a rhythm of rebuilding by day and revelry by dark.
26.inhabitants: The large bug-eyed lizards of Legees govern themselves through a loose confederacy of farming settlements, each holding its own council and pooling resources only when quakes demand it. Modest tools and getting-by wealth keep most of the population tied to the land, but the same lizards who spend their days resetting irrigation channels and shoring up walls are known to spend their nights running the taverns, gaming houses and dance-floors that outsiders travel to see. Practical and unshaken by disaster, they treat both farming and nightlife as necessary work.

27.description: Quator's surface is given over to smelting works and refineries strung along its river valleys, their output moved by rail gangs that answer to no central authority. Without a government to enforce order, the factories operate under shifting local arrangements between foremen, guilds, and armed cooperatives. The world's peculiar notoriety comes from bands of edible arts graduates, trained in culinary guilds elsewhere and turned loose here, who roam the industrial districts staging poisonings and sabotage dressed up as haute cuisine. Settlements are modest in size and spaced along the transit lines, built more for function than comfort.
27.inhabitants: The colonials who work Quator's foundries and yards are practical people, used to settling disputes and dividing labor without recourse to any higher authority. Wages are thin and conditions plain, and most treat the wandering graduates and their poisoned banquets as an occupational hazard to be watched for rather than a mystery to be solved.

28.description: Arexe is a large industrial world whose factory districts ring cities built upward rather than outward, a concession to population pressure rather than aesthetics. Its studios produce sit coms distributed across neighboring space, an irony not lost on a citizenry that has despised the form since long before the current broadcast towers were raised. Advanced automation keeps the industrial base humming quietly enough that most residential quarters remain untouched by smoke or noise.
28.inhabitants: The furry rodent population governs itself through elected councils that argue endlessly and, by most accounts, competently, producing a wealthy and orderly society with little patience for frivolity. Their contempt for sit coms runs deep and generational, yet the export trade persists because someone else's amusement pays the bills, a contradiction the locals discuss with weary humor rather than embarrassment.

29.description: Atrabiin is a small world of cramped foundries and smoke-blackened refineries, its industry never quite recovering from whatever slump left it poor. The land beyond the settlements belongs to the Esisoids, a wild growth harvested for food despite a long, well-documented history of killing those who process it wrong. Refining sheds for the Esisoid crop sit apart from the smelting districts, ringed with warnings and burn-scarred ground where past mistakes are still visible. Each settlement answers to its own local authority, and none has managed to outlaw the harvest outright, only to regulate around it.
29.inhabitants: The Horned Lobsters who work Atrabiin split their labor between ore and Esisoid processing, and carry the burns and old poisonings of both trades as a matter of course. Fractured rule among competing local governments means safety practice varies sharply from one settlement to the next, and workers judge a place as much by its Esisoid-handling reputation as by its wages. Getting by is the general condition, and most treat the crop's danger as an old, familiar cost of living rather than a thing worth remarking on.

30.description: Usanat spreads across broad, quiet plains given over almost entirely to grain and root crops, tended in collective plots that repeat with little variation from one horizon to the next. Its settlements are small and far apart, connected by dirt roads and the occasional rail spur used to move harvests to the central depots. Nothing of note has happened here in living memory, and the world's reputation for dullness is treated locally less as an insult than as a simple statement of fact.
30.inhabitants: The colonials work fixed quotas on state-assigned land, their days shaped by planting and harvest cycles rather than ambition or event. Officials rotate through the collective farms enforcing production targets with primitive tools and little fanfare, and conversation tends toward crop yields, weather, and the slow turning of the calendar.

31.description: Xeesle is a small world given over to industrial estates held by hereditary lords, its low hills cut with tramways and cooling ponds. The workshops turn out plate stock and simple castings, shipped between holdings under terms set generations ago and rarely revised. Little distinguishes one district from the next, and travellers who pass through report finding no reason to linger; even the weather here keeps to a narrow, unremarkable range.
31.inhabitants: The colonials work the foundries and smallholds their families have held under the same lords for as long as anyone can trace, and take a certain pride in the steadiness of it. Wealth is modest and closely managed, and ambition tends to run toward keeping a workshop rather than expanding one.

32.description: Oreseren's industrial districts sit under a permanent haze of smelter smoke, the runoff from its foundries staining rivers a dull grey-brown that never fully clears. Refuse piles accumulate at the edges of holdings faster than anyone bothers to clear them, and the smell of processing plants carries for a considerable distance across the lowlands. The world's factories serve the estates of its lords, turning out goods with little regard for what is left behind.
32.inhabitants: Labor here answers to hereditary holders who claim the foundries and the land alike, leaving workers with little say over conditions they endure daily. Most get by on what the estates allow them, hardened to the grime and stink of their trade rather than troubled by it.

33.description: Inera's landmass is dominated by refineries and processing yards, their heat-exchange towers rising above the coastal cities like a second skyline. Yet the wealth here comes as much from the sea as from the smelters: the temperate shelf waters that ring the continents are farmed and netted for fish stocks found nowhere else, prized for meat unlike anything raised on a standard agricultural world. Settlement is dense and continuous along the coasts, thinning inland toward the industrial belts that feed the export docks. The corporate charters that administer the planet have shaped both shoreline and skyline to their own efficient design.
33.inhabitants: Most Inerans work under contract to one of the great combines, whether on the factory floors or aboard the licensed fishing fleets, and company loyalty runs as deep as any civic identity. Life is comfortable and orderly by advanced-world standards, but promotion, housing and even leisure time are allocated through corporate hierarchy rather than left to chance.

34.description: Inus spreads across a wide, thinly populated expanse of forest and broken ground, its low-tech farmsteads scattered rather than clustered because the land beneath them cannot be trusted to hold still. Fault lines run under the tree cover, and unpredictable earthquakes have flattened outbuildings and reshaped the same valleys more than once. The Inusian tree wolf, a lean predator adapted to the shifting terrain, is the one thing outsiders are likely to have heard of before anything else about the place. Farming continues on the strength of habit and necessity rather than any confidence in the ground.
34.inhabitants: The colonials of Inus live in small, self-reliant holdings under a dictatorship that has little presence beyond the collection of tribute and the occasional show of force. Generations of tremors have made them practical about property and quick to rebuild rather than mourn, and most families keep half an eye on the tree line where the wolves range.

35.description: Isence spreads across a large world whose industrial districts ring the equator in overlapping jurisdictions, each holding its own charter, tariffs, and law. Its casinos, built into refinery towers and old orbital-shipment terminals, are famous for games found nowhere else, drawing custom even as a persistent wasting sickness moves through the lower-city wards. Quarantine lines and sealed transit tubes now cut across the gaming floors, so that fortune and contagion share the same corridors. The factories keep running regardless, their output too valuable for any one government to halt for the sake of the sick.
35.inhabitants: The population answers to whichever authority holds their district, and loyalties shift block by block rather than along any single line of rule. Industrial labor and casino trade have made most residents comfortable, but the disease has bred a wary fatalism, and many carry sealed passes and personal filtration gear as routinely as identification. Physicians, actuaries, and gaming-house wardens hold unusual local standing, since all three profit from calculating how long a person, or a table, is likely to last.

36.description: Reesdice is a large world of shallow seas and broad river deltas, its landmass given over almost entirely to collective farms and aquaculture pens. The coastal shoals harbor the Reesdician lobstoid, a heavily armored predator whose venomous claw has made the creature both a local hazard and the world's chief claim to notice beyond its own sky. Settlement clusters in fortified river towns rather than along the open coast, where the lobstoid beds make shoreline living an unwise habit. Grain barges and processing sheds dominate what industry the world possesses, most of it modest in scale and state-run.
36.inhabitants: The lizard population lives under a planned economy that assigns labor to the collective farms, the river fisheries, and the wary harvesting crews who bring in lobstoid meat and shell under strict quota. Life is plain and workmanlike, shaped more by the demands of soil and tide than by any comfort of wealth, and most households get by on ration and routine rather than surplus. A caution about open water is bred into them early, and it shows in how the towns are built and how the young are taught to swim.

37.description: Terea is a large world given over almost entirely to state-run agriculture, its broad plains and river deltas divided into collective holdings that stretch to the horizon in every direction. The soil and long growing season have made it famous across the region for the Tereaian edible poet, a delicacy cultivated nowhere else with the same success. Settlements are few and spread thin, each built around a central granary or processing works, with modest tooling and machinery doing what labor cannot.
37.inhabitants: The Black Slimy Rodents native to Terea work the collective farms under a planned economy that assigns quota and ration alike, and generations of this arrangement have bred a population patient with hardship and suspicious of anything that smells of private gain. Getting by rather than thriving, they take a quiet, proprietary pride in the poet harvest, treating its cultivation as a shared achievement of the whole world rather than any single farm.

38.description: Orgetibe spreads across a wide, unremarkable land of low hills and grey scrubland, most of it given over to thin, laborious farming that barely feeds the scattered holdings dependent on it. No single authority governs the world; instead a patchwork of local chiefdoms and township councils divides the land, none strong enough to build much beyond its own borders. Settlements are few and far between, mud-walled and timber-roofed, separated by long stretches of empty pasture and untended field. Traders and record-keepers alike agree there is little here to remark upon beyond the sameness of it all.
38.inhabitants: The black furry felines who work this soil are plain, practical folk, bound more to their own village councils than to any wider notion of a planet. Generations of primitive tools and poor harvests have made them cautious and self-reliant, distrustful of grand promises and unimpressed by outsiders. What little they have, they keep close, and what they lack, they do without.

39.description: Reorte is a large world of unstable ground, its farmland belts crossed by fault lines that shift without warning and level whole villages. Settlements are built low and wide, of timber and packed earth rather than stone, so that when the tremors come the walls fall without killing everyone beneath them. Despite the risk, or perhaps because of it, the world has cultivated a peculiar reputation as a welcoming stop for outsiders, with guesthouses and viewing platforms built along the fault scarps themselves. The dictatorship that rules the place directs most surplus grain toward feeding the cities rather than repairing what the earth breaks.
39.inhabitants: The Black Fat Felines who work Reorte's fields are broad, heavy-built people, suited to labor in low gravity pockets near the rift zones where the soil is richest. Generations of loss have made them fatalistic about the ground beneath them, and this same fatalism has curdled into an odd hospitality, a delight in showing outsiders the cracked earth and telling them what it has taken. Under the dictatorship's tight allocation of land and grain, most families measure a good year simply by the number of quakes it did not bring.

40.description: Ququor's farmland stretches across shallow river basins and warm coastal plains, given over almost entirely to the crops and livestock that feed its export kitchens. Settlements are arranged around processing depots and distribution warehouses owned by the agricultural concerns that administer the world, with dining districts built up around each one to serve the trade that follows. Its cuisine, built on ingredients found nowhere in quite the same combination, has earned the world a name that outstrips its modest size.
40.inhabitants: The native lizards, docile and slow-moving, are farmed alongside conventional stock and figure heavily in the dishes that give the world its reputation. Most people work under contract to the estates and processing firms that structure daily life, and a comfortable living is the norm rather than the exception, though ambition tends to run toward the corporate ladder rather than anything else.

41.description: Geinona orbits close enough to its star that flares strip the upper atmosphere on an irregular cycle, scouring exposed structures and forcing most industry underground or into shielded halls. Refineries and forges cluster in deep galleries cut into the bedrock, their stacks venting through baffled shafts to survive the surges. Above ground, settlements are compact and low, built to be sealed at short notice, and much of the small world's surface bears the scorched, glassy scars of past storms.
41.inhabitants: Households and workshops answer to hereditary lords who control the shielded galleries and ration access to safe working hours around each storm cycle. Life is a matter of endurance rather than comfort, with most colonials laboring long shifts in the deep foundries and holding little beyond what the season's flares allow them to keep.

42.description: Anarlaqu is a wide, thinly settled world where the soil gives up little and the estates of the landholders stretch far beyond what their tenants can till. What passes for wealth here is spent on the evening hours: the fields empty at dusk and the manor courts light their lanterns for dances, gambling and drink that draw talk from well beyond the parish. The rest of the world's business is small, slow and conducted on foot or by cart, under lords who tax the harvest and tolerate little else.
42.inhabitants: Most people here are bound to a plot and a patron, working land that barely feeds them under masters who take the greater share. The night gatherings are the one place where field hands, freeholders and gentry mix loosely, and colonials speak of them as the only fair trade this world offers.

43.description: Oresri's broad temperate belts hold rich soil that yields grain and fodder crops far beyond what its own population can consume, but the fields lie divided along shifting front lines. Collective farms and grain silos dot the plains, many now abandoned or fought over as the civil war drags between rival communes and provincial cadres. Rail lines built to move harvest to the ports are cut and rerouted as territory changes hands, and modest workshops turn from making harvest equipment to arms with little transition. The world remains sizeable and fertile enough that even divided factions have never quite starved out their rivals.
43.inhabitants: The rodent population, once organized under strict collectivist doctrine, now splits its labor between tending fields and defending them, with local committees enforcing rationing and conscription in equal measure. Life expectancy and comfort vary sharply by district depending on which faction holds the granaries that season. Even so, most communities keep working the land out of necessity, trusting that harvests will outlast whichever government claims to speak for them.

44.description: Esesla spreads across a considerable landmass under scattered farming holdings, its low-tech settlements strung out with wide, empty tracts of cultivated land between them. The world lacks any single ruling authority, its territories instead divided among competing local governments that rarely agree on much beyond boundary lines. Its odd claim to note is the Zero-G hockey circuit run out of orbital cages above the farm belts, a pastime far removed from the modest fields below.
44.inhabitants: The population, small black rodents adapted to a life of manual labour, work scattered plots under governments too fractured and too poor to invest in much beyond subsistence. What wealth exists tends to be spent on maintaining the orbital rinks rather than on the primitive tools of the fields, a source of some resentment among the farming holds.

45.description: Socelage carries broad temperate lowlands given over to pasture and mixed cropland, broken by ranges of low hills where herds graze on wild scrub. The world's holdings are divided among modest freehold farms rather than great estates, and its exotic goat meat has built a reputation felt well past the local market towns. Grain silos and stockyards dominate the outskirts of every settlement, while the town centers keep to the plain, unfortified architecture typical of a world that has never needed to plan for siege.
45.inhabitants: The colonials who work these farms hold to elected councils at every level, from parish boards to the planetary assembly, and take a proprietary pride in the animals and pastures each family tends. Comfortable rather than affluent, they favor practical dress and plain speech, and the goat herders in particular are regarded, even by outsiders, as the shrewdest breeders in their region.

46.description: Riedquat is a large world of thin farmsteads scattered across broad, unclaimed plains, its holdings too far apart to answer to any single authority. What order exists is local and temporary, and the countryside is periodically torn by feuds between settlements that flare into open fighting before subsiding into uneasy truce. Despite the poverty and disorder, the kitchens of Riedquat have earned a reputation far out of proportion to the planet's means, built on slow-cooked grains, wild greens and whatever meat the season allows.
46.inhabitants: Farmers and cooks make up most of the population, working small plots with hand tools and passing recipes down as carefully as land. Lacking any central government to arbitrate disputes, communities settle grievances among themselves, sometimes with words and sometimes with raids, but a shared pride in the table tends to outlast any quarrel.

47.description: Gerege is a small world whose land area cannot support its heavy population, forcing settlements upward into tiered blocks stacked along the reclaimed hill country of the northern belt. Its industry is old and inefficient, running on advanced tooling that outpaces the poor ore and thin farmland the world actually offers, so wealth here comes from finance and export trade rather than what is dug or grown locally. The remaining wild country, kept deliberately undeveloped by confederal decree, shelters the Geregian spotted wolf, and the animal has become the subject of study, tourism pamphlets, and no small civic pride.
47.inhabitants: The population, descended from colonial stock, is dense, well-off, and governed through a confederacy of settlement councils that argue endlessly over land allocation and industrial quotas. Most work is administrative or technical, done indoors in cramped, advanced facilities, and the wolf reserves are among the few places where anyone has room to walk without a schedule.

48.description: Usle's continents are given over to processing and assembly, with refineries and fabrication yards spreading across its lowland basins under a permanent haze of exhaust. Vast tracts of managed forest ring the industrial belts, host to the Uslian tree ant, a species studied and exported by entomologists and curiosity collectors alike. Settlement runs continuous along the coasts and river deltas, factory housing giving way to civic halls where the member territories of the confederacy send their delegates to argue over production quotas.
48.inhabitants: The small black felines who populate Usle organise their labour through the confederacy's endless committees, taking evident pride in consensus reached the hard way. Comfortable wages and steady work have left them opinionated and unhurried, and their well-documented contempt for sit coms is aired often and without embarrassment in the local broadcasts.

49.description: Malama's continents are given over almost entirely to refineries, shipyards and processing plants, their smoke and light visible across whole regions after dark. Beneath the industrial haze, terraced growing domes and coastal aquaculture pens supply the ingredients behind the world's reputation for exotic cuisine, a soft counterpoint to the metal sprawl around them. Cities here are built in concentric rings around their factories, with housing blocks stacked close and function dictating almost every street.
49.inhabitants: The population works long, regimented shifts under a government that plans output and rationing alike, and prosperity here is real but distributed strictly along lines the state draws. Off duty, Malamans take unusual pride in their cooking, treating rare ingredients and inventive preparation as one of the few forms of personal expression the system does not regulate.

50.description: Aesbion's cities form continuous industrial belts across its lowlands, refineries and fabrication plants running day and night behind fences that mark the true borders of the world. Corporate charters divide the planet into holdings rather than nations, and it is these holdings that now fight one another for control of ore fields and orbital yards. The civil war has not slowed production so much as bent it toward armament, with factory output redirected to shells and hull plate faster than to anything sold openly offworld.
50.inhabitants: Most residents work under contract to whichever holding administers their district, and loyalty tends to follow the paycheck rather than any wider cause. Long exposure to factional fighting has left people practical and guarded, quick to note which checkpoints belong to which corporate militia before saying much at all.

51.description: Alaza spreads across broad temperate plains and river deltas given over almost entirely to grain and root crops, its farms organized into wide cooperative holdings that stretch to the horizon. The world's fields and packed lowland settlements have long served as breeding ground for a persistent and virulent disease, one that has resisted every quarantine line and every planting season's hope that it might have finally burned itself out. Clinics and isolation wards are as much a fixture of the rural townships as grain silos, and entire districts rotate through cycles of lockdown and harvest. Despite this, the agricultural output continues largely uninterrupted, the population too large and too dependent on the land to abandon it.
51.inhabitants: The population, harmless bug-eyed birds by nature, organizes itself through elected councils and open assemblies even in the depths of quarantine, debating relief measures and planting quotas with the same open contentiousness. Comfortable but unremarkable wealth keeps most households provided for, and the long, thankless work of the sick-wards is treated as a shared civic duty rather than a specialist's burden. There is a settled, communal endurance to them, born of generations spent farming through recurring outbreaks without ever leaving the land.

52.description: Xeaqu is a small world of flat grain country and slow rivers, its fields worked with hand tools and draft animals rather than machinery. There is no capital, no seat of government, and no record of anything remarkable ever having happened here. Farmsteads sit far apart across the plains, each tending its own plot and its own affairs, and the sameness of the land from one horizon to the next has given the world its reputation.
52.inhabitants: Without any ruling authority, the colonials settle disputes among themselves, plot by plot, and keep mostly to their own kin. Life follows the planting and harvest with little variation from one season to the next, and few here expect, or want, anything to change that.

53.description: Raoror's landscape is broken by volcanic cones that vent gas and ash in irregular fits, giving the world its wide reputation among traders and geologists alike. The settlements cluster along ridgelines and old lava terraces, well back from the vents, in patchwork districts built from salvaged industrial plate and hardened slag brick. Factories here run without central oversight, cobbled together and re-cobbled as ownership of each smokestack changes hands or simply gets forgotten. There is no single authority to plan around the mountains, so the towns grow toward whichever slope last stopped erupting.
53.inhabitants: The Bug-Eyed Frogs of Raoror organize their labor through shifting local pacts rather than any lasting government, trading loyalty for shelter and machine parts as circumstances demand. Generations of getting by amid unpredictable ground have made them practical and watchful, quick to abandon a district when the vents nearby start acting strange. Industrial work is steady but never secure, and most keep at least one bag packed against the next migration.

54.description: Ororqu's factories and habitation blocks spread across a landmass regularly scoured by solar flares, and much of the surface architecture is built low and shielded against radiation surges that arrive with little warning. Despite this, the world has grown wealthy on steady industrial output, its cities dense with housing and manufacturing districts wired together against outages. The ancient mating rites of its people, conducted in fixed seasonal gatherings regardless of the weather overhead, draw notice from beyond the system and give the place its lasting reputation.
54.inhabitants: The rodent population governs itself through open democratic assembly, favoring practical compromise over ceremony in most civic matters. Generations of coping with solar disruption have made them methodical and unhurried in crisis, though their devotion to the old courtship customs remains fixed and unshaken by circumstance.

55.description: Leesti is a small world whose thin arable margins long ago gave way to close-packed industrial districts, run by charter and contract rather than open ground. The corporate boards that own its factories also own the arenas where Zero-G cricket is played, and matches draw crowds from every tier of the vertical cities. Its distilleries produce the notoriously potent Leestian evil juice, brewed in vats beside the same plants that turn out the world's poor-grade industrial goods, a contrast the boards have never bothered to resolve.
55.inhabitants: The population lives under corporate charter, with housing, employment and leisure all administered by the same handful of firms, and most residents hold shares or debts to whichever board runs their district. Wealth sits visibly alongside crowding, and the evident polish of company towers does little to hide the poor industrial base beneath them. Leestians take fierce pride in their cricket leagues and their liquor, treating both as proof that something of theirs remains outside the boards' ledgers.

56.description: Geisgeza is a small world of thin, rocky ground and oceans that lie strange to the eye, colored and layered in ways unlike waters found elsewhere. Its farms cling to terraced highland slopes above the coasts, working soil that gives little back. The Geisgezaian mountain slug, a slow armored grazer of the upper ridges, is the planet's chief curiosity and a fixture of local diet and folklore alike. Settlements are scattered and small, tied together by unpaved roads and the authority of a single ruling hand.
56.inhabitants: Life under the dictatorship is hard and closely watched, with most labor bent toward wringing food from poor land and gathering slug meat and shell from the mountains. The colonials are plain-spoken and self-reliant, accustomed to shortage and to keeping their opinions of the government to themselves.

57.description: Zainlabi's factory districts and refineries operate under a haze that never quite clears, the industrial base shifting hands as control of the world changes without warning. Confederacy administration nominally governs the planet, but its authority runs only as far as whichever faction currently holds the production centers, and the front lines redraw themselves across the settled belts with little notice. Infrastructure built for orderly output now serves whoever last took the district, and the skyline of any given city may bear the scars of the most recent turnover.
57.inhabitants: The population works the mills and yards under contracts that outlast any single government, switching allegiance as often as the fighting demands and treating the disruption as a cost of doing business rather than a crisis. Comfortable wealth persists despite the chaos, sustained by an industrial output too valuable for any faction to let stand idle for long.

58.description: Uscela's continents are given over almost entirely to grain belts, orchard terraces and irrigated pasture, the horizon broken only by silos and the low ridgelines between one farm cooperative and the next. Its climate is even, its seasons predictable, and its towns follow the same grid plan from one province to the next, laid out for efficient transport of harvests rather than for variety. Travellers and locals alike describe it as an unremarkable place, and little in its recent history contradicts them; nothing here has burned, failed, or risen dramatically in living memory.
58.inhabitants: The population lives comfortably under a confederacy of agricultural cooperatives, each province sending representatives to argue mildly about quotas and irrigation rights. Generations of steady, unspectacular plenty have bred a people who are practical, mild-tempered, and largely content to let their world remain exactly as dull as it has always been.

59.description: Isveve spreads wide and thin, its arable belts broken by long stretches of untended scrub where no clan holds claim. Farmsteads sit apart from one another by design rather than accident, each cut off from its neighbours by fences, hedgerows, or simply distance. What passes for a market town is little more than a cluster of shuttered stalls that opens for a few hours at dawn and closes again before anyone lingers. The soil gives enough to live on, but little tooling exists to take more from it than a family can manage alone.
59.inhabitants: With no authority above the household to compel gathering, the colonials of Isveve have settled into a habit of withdrawal, trading through drop-boxes and hand signals rather than conversation. Strangers are met with closed doors and averted eyes long before any threat is shown, and even neighbours of long standing keep their exchanges short and their fences high. The eccentric shyness noted of them is less fear than custom, a quiet inherited from generations who found isolation safer than trust.

60.description: Tioranin's farmland spreads across gentle river basins that once fed a modest export trade, though much of the acreage now lies fallow or burned where fighting has passed through. The world is best known off-planet for its vicious brew, a harsh spirit distilled in small batches by farmers who have kept the recipe going through repeated upheavals. Settlements are dense but patched together, walls rebuilt more than once, and the countryside between them shifts hands as the civil war ebbs and flares without settling into any lasting front.
60.inhabitants: The population elects its councils faithfully even as those councils struggle to hold authority beyond the town they sit in, and loyalty tends to run to neighbours and distillers rather than to any distant government. Comfortable enough to eat well between disruptions, Tioraninians are practical and wary, quick to hide stores and quicker to argue politics, having learned that both the harvest and the peace can be taken away without much warning.”}

61.description: Learorce is a small world whose land surface is given over largely to dense, unbroken forest, broken only by the scattered clearings where its industry has taken root. The timber and processing works that anchor the economy sit apart from one another, connected by long cuts through the woods rather than any single road network. The forests themselves are the world's chief distinction, though local report holds them to be scourged by a strain of deadly edible poets, a hazard as much discussed as the trees themselves. Settlement is thin, with modest industrial holdings standing isolated amid the timber rather than gathered into any real town.
61.inhabitants: The large rodents who work Learorce answer to no single authority, the world being divided among competing local governments that each administer their own logging concessions and mills. Life here is a matter of getting by rather than prospering, and the workforce is practical and wary, trained by necessity to treat anything gathered from the forest floor with suspicion before it reaches a plate.

62.description: Esusti's industrial belts ring its temperate lowlands, feeding a population housed in dense, state-planned blocks that spread across the sizeable landmass. The world is well known for the Esustian spotted cat, bred and kept across every district, and for an ancient, near-institutional loathing of discos, a prejudice old enough to have shaped the design of its public halls. No licensed dance establishment on the planet plays past a certain hour, and none features a mirrored floor.
62.inhabitants: Esustians work in state-run manufacturing collectives, disciplined and comfortable under a wealthy communist administration that keeps its cities well supplied and its factories humming. Off duty they keep spotted cats as a matter of civic pride and speak of an old cultural grudge against disco music with more seriousness than most outsiders expect.

63.description: Ususor spreads wide and lightly settled, its holdings given over to thin fields worked by hand under the authority of local lords. Farms cluster around fortified manors separated by long stretches of open, unclaimed ground. The world's chief oddity is the Ususorian edible poet, a cultivated organism prized locally and served at feast and tribute alike, its name a source of endless confusion to outsiders who expect verse rather than a dish.
63.inhabitants: The people keep to themselves, retreating from strangers with a shyness remarked upon across the settled worlds, a habit bred by scattered farmsteads and the closed, hierarchical demands of feudal service. Loyalty runs to the local manor rather than to any distant crown, and conversation with those outside the household comes slowly, if it comes at all.

64.description: Maregeis pairs heavy manufacturing districts with the ancient Soenor tulip plantations that first gave the world its name off-world, the two economies existing in an uneasy border along the low hill country. Factory towns rise in blocks of grey stone and iron near the equatorial coalfields, their smoke drifting inland to darken the petals of fields that have been tended by the same families for longer than any local record can confirm. Settlement is thin and scattered outside these two centers, with much of the sizeable landmass left to scrub and tidal flat.
64.inhabitants: The small black slimy lobsters who work the plantations and forges answer to hereditary holders who claim the land by old right rather than purchase, and most labor is owed rather than paid. Life among the tulip rows is regarded as the better inheritance, and families that hold plantation rights guard them jealously against relatives bound instead to the foundries. Wealth here is modest and unevenly held, and most get by on what the soil or the furnace allows rather than what either produces in surplus.

65.description: Aate's industry sprawls across highland basins and terraced slopes, its refineries and processing towers cut into the same mountain chains that shelter the killer lobstoids for which the world is infamous. Settlements cluster behind graded perimeters and reinforced approach roads, a defensive geography as much as an industrial one. Wealth here is measured in output tonnage moved down from the highlands to the lowland ports, past ground that is never entirely safe to walk unescorted.
65.inhabitants: The corporate charters that govern Aate treat the lobstoid ranges as a managed cost of production, rostering hardened crews for highland work and paying accordingly. Colonials born to the industry towns grow up practical and unsentimental about the mountains, aware that the company ledger and the casualty list are kept by the same office.

66.description: Sori's farmland spreads across broad river basins under a government that assigns quotas for every field and granary. The world's agricultural wealth has long supported dense settlement, but a persistent and ill-understood disease moves through the population in slow, recurring waves, and entire districts are periodically sealed off by decree while it runs its course. Grain silos and quarantine walls stand side by side in most towns, a permanent feature of the landscape rather than an emergency measure. Even so, the harvests continue, and the markets and granaries remain full behind their checkpoints.
66.inhabitants: The Fierce Black Lizards native to Sori are disciplined and wary, shaped by generations of curfews, quotas, and quarantine drills imposed from above. Farming families work under close supervision, and a habit of terse, guarded speech has become the norm even among neighbors, born from years of watching for the next outbreak and the next official response to it.

67.description: Cemave's crust is restless, riven by fault lines that shrug the surface into fresh ridges and sinkholes with grim regularity. Its factories and refineries are built low and reinforced, spread across wide plains rather than raised into towers, a concession the world's many competing administrations reached only after repeated collapses. The industrial output remains heavy and constant even as districts are periodically rebuilt, and the world is known across the region chiefly for the dreadful earthquakes that never quite let it rest.
67.inhabitants: The fierce black insects that hold Cemave answer to no single authority, their nests and hives organized instead under a patchwork of rival governments that divide the industrial plains between them. Generations of tremors have bred a population that treats structural collapse as routine business, quick to swarm toward damage and just as quick to resume production once it is cleared. Comfortable wealth has not softened them; it has simply given every faction more machinery worth defending.

68.description: Arusqudi's oceans dominate the world's reputation, their color and chemistry unlike those of any neighboring system, drawing scholars and curiosity alone rather than trade. Collective farms ring the coastlines, their fields laid out in state-mandated grids that feed the populous settlements further inland. The technology is modest, machinery kept running past its intended years, and the agricultural output is steady rather than remarkable. Most towns cluster near processing stations where the harvest is weighed, recorded and distributed according to quota.
68.inhabitants: The small bug-eyed lobsters that populate Arusqudi work under a rigid collective system, laboring on assigned plots and drawing rations that leave most getting by without great want or great comfort. Generations of central planning have made them patient, methodical, and unshowy, more inclined to discuss the strange tides than to speak of politics. Those who study the oceans do so as an approved diversion from the otherwise uniform rhythm of farm life.

69.description: Eredve is a small world whose foundries and refineries operate at reduced capacity, their output diminished by the chronic epidemic that has settled into the population and refuses to lift. Quarantine walls partition the older manufacturing districts from the newer housing blocks, a division that has hardened into the permanent shape of the settlements. State clinics and isolation wards occupy as much ground as the assembly halls they were built to serve, and the smoke above the stacks carries the smell of disinfectant along with industrial exhaust.
69.inhabitants: The insectoid population labors under collective directives that treat sickness as a production problem to be managed rather than a private grief, and hive-councils rotate workers between factory floor and sickbay with the same flat efficiency. Despite the toll, the colony holds to a stubborn, communal discipline, its comfortable material provision funding an endless, grinding effort to keep the plague from ever quite winning.

70.description: Regeatge is a large world whose continents are covered in great dense forests, broken only by cleared belts of farmland around scattered settlements. Its agricultural economy is unremarkable in what it produces, but the timber and cleared ground are worth fighting over, and the world has no single authority to stop that fighting. Competing local governments hold overlapping and disputed territories, and the forests themselves have absorbed generations of skirmish lines and abandoned outposts. Settlement remains moderate, with towns kept small and defensible rather than allowed to spread into the woodland.
70.inhabitants: The population lives under whichever local government holds their district this season, and loyalty tends to follow the nearest garrison rather than any distant capital. Farmers work the cleared land with one eye on the tree line, aware that militias move through the forest with as much ease as game animals. Poverty and modest technology mean most disputes are settled with old equipment and older grudges, and the colonials who remain are those too rooted to their fields to leave.

71.description: Edinso's lowlands are given over to vast terraced plantations of pink Ontivediweed, their rows running to the horizon between processing towns and the industrial belts that refine and ship the crop onward. Beyond the cultivated valleys the terrain rises into forested highlands where mountain monkey troops have grown bold and numerous enough to strip fields, raid stores, and force the abandonment of several outlying plantations. Wealth from weed exports and steady manufacturing has built dense, orderly settlements across the lowlands, their skylines a mix of refineries and tightly packed housing blocks under a single, unyielding authority.
71.inhabitants: The Black Horned Lizards who work the plantations and factory floors do so under a dictatorship that directs labour and land use with little appeal, and this has bred a population that is disciplined, guarded in speech, and quick to defer to whoever holds local authority. Generations of monkey incursions into the highland farms have also left plantation crews pragmatic and armed for the work, treating the loss of a field as a cost of doing business rather than a crisis.

72.description: Ra is a small world whose thin crust never sits still for long, its farming districts laid out in low, quake-braced terraces rather than fixed towns. Fields of hardy grain and root crops are worked with primitive tools between tremors, and much of the architecture is squat, single-storey and built to fall without killing those inside it. The corporate charter that administers Ra keeps its holdings scattered across several fault zones, so that no single collapse can ruin a season's yield outright.
72.inhabitants: The large black bony lobsters who work Ra's terraces answer to company overseers who set quotas without much regard for the ground's temper, and life here is measured out in aftershocks and harvests rather than seasons. They are a practical, unsentimental people, quick to rebuild and slow to trust anything that stands taller than a single storey.

73.description: Aronar's industry is old and half-worn, its foundries and refineries scattered across a landscape of grazing highlands and low grey mills under feudal writ. The Aronarian deadly goat, bred wild in the upland scrub, is prized and feared in equal measure across the settled districts, while the casinos of the lowland towns draw those willing to risk what little wealth they hold. Manor holdings ring the industrial belts, each lord answering to custom rather than any distant charter, and the world's fortunes rise and fall with ore prices and the gambling houses' luck.
73.inhabitants: The small furry insect population lives under strict feudal obligation, laborers and artisans bound to their holdings even as the casinos offer a rare, chaotic escape from that order. Herders who tend the deadly goats are regarded with a wary respect, their trade dangerous and their status oddly elevated for a world otherwise governed by rank and inheritance.

74.description: Arraesso's oceans run strange colors and heavier tides than charts expect, a consequence of mineral saturation that has never been fully explained by the handful of scholars who bother to visit. Settlements cling to the coastal shelves in scattered clusters, thin farming villages linked by dirt roads and the occasional feudal keep. The soil is poor and the growing season short, so most holdings scrape by on hardy grain and salt-fish rather than anything worth shipping offworld.
74.inhabitants: Life under the local lords is hard and closely watched, with most labor going straight to tithe and subsistence rather than surplus. The people hold a fierce, almost proverbial hatred of food blenders, a grudge tied to some old story about spoiled ocean harvests that every household still repeats as fact. They are plain-spoken folk, suspicious of machinery in the kitchen and loyal above all to their own patch of shoreline.

75.description: Cevege's factory belts ring the equator in an unbroken smear of smoke and effluent, feeding refineries that never fully shut down. Wealth accumulates in state coffers faster than sanitation can keep pace with production, and the heavily populated hive-cities sit under a permanent haze of industrial runoff. Canals meant to carry waste away from the manufacturing districts have long since become open sewers, and the smell is a byword across the trade routes for what advanced technology looks like when nothing is spent on appearances.
75.inhabitants: The insectile population organizes labor through rigid collective hierarchies, every caste assigned to production quotas set by the central committee. Fierce by temperament and unsentimental about squalor, they regard the filth of their hives as an acceptable cost of output and treat complaints about it as a foreign affectation.

76.description: Orteve's continents are given over almost entirely to refineries, distilleries, and the housing blocks that serve them, with the skyline broken by cooling towers rather than any natural feature. The world's fame rests on the Leaer gargle blaster, a drink brewed and bottled in vast quantities across competing municipal districts, each claiming the authentic recipe. Ownership of the planet is split among a patchwork of local administrations, none of which controls the whole trade, so the industrial districts operate under different codes and inspection regimes depending on which sector of the world a plant sits in.
76.inhabitants: The Black Fat Humanoids who work the distilleries and packing lines are known for a dry humor about their own product, treating its viciousness as a point of civic pride rather than a hazard. Life under the divided administrations has made them practiced negotiators, used to shifting paperwork and permits between jurisdictions that share a planet but little else, and comfortable wealth has left them more concerned with quality of the brew than with strict adherence to any one government's rules.

77.description: Geerra is a small world of modest farms and pasture, its low hills terraced with fodder crops and dotted with goat herds that give the place its name in trader circles. Settlements are loosely spread across the arable belts, small enough that most business is still conducted face to face. The planet's reputation rests almost entirely on its exotic goat soup, a dish worked into local ceremony and served at gatherings of every kind. Beyond the herding and the soup pots, technology here remains basic, and most tools and buildings show the wear of long, careful use rather than replacement.
77.inhabitants: The colonials of Geerra vote on most matters that touch the community, from grazing rights to festival dates, and take a plain pride in settling things themselves rather than deferring to any distant authority. Life is unhurried but not easy, and households get by through steady herding, shared labor, and the recipes passed down for the soup that visitors and neighbors alike have come to expect at any table worth sitting at.

78.description: Soinuste's crust is restless, riven by fault lines that bring collapse to whatever is built too tall or too permanent.
