Its industry survives in low, heavily braced sheds scattered far apart, a pattern forced by both the shaking ground and the absence of any authority to plan otherwise. Refineries and foundries are patched rather than rebuilt, their output modest and their machinery older than it should be. What settlements exist sit on the more stable ground between fault lines, thin strings of habitation rather than towns.
78.inhabitants: The insects that hold this world are large, armored, and given to loud territorial displays that look far more dangerous than they are, since none of their posturing carries any real sting. Without government to coordinate rebuilding or relief, each cluster of workers manages its own sheds and shelters, distrustful of outsiders and quick to bristle but rarely violent in fact. Generations of tremors have taught them to build low, live light, and expect to lose what they make.

79.description: Erlage is a small world given over almost entirely to industry, its cramped landmass covered in refineries, foundries and the dense residential blocks needed to house a population far larger than its size would suggest. Between the industrial belts, patches of managed forest survive, home to the Erlagian tree ant, cultivated and studied for its role in the world's minor but persistent reputation as something other than a factory floor. The uplands are another matter: steep, unwelcoming, and infested with mountain goats whose aggression toward workers and livestock alike has made the high slopes effectively abandoned to them.
79.inhabitants: The population lives well by the standards of industrial worlds, its wealth spread widely enough under the Confederacy's power-sharing councils that most colonials hold a stake, however small, in the refineries and manufactories around them. Erlagians are practical, unsentimental people, quick to complain about the goat problem in the abstract while treating the tree ant with something close to civic pride.

80.description: Xeaan packs its factories and refineries into a tight ring of cities crowded onto a small landmass, the confederacy's constituent councils each holding a district and a share of production. Civil war moves through the world in fits and starts, flaring over a foundry or a transit line and then subsiding into uneasy truce, so that the same street can be a battle line one season and a market the next. Smoke-blackened quarters sit alongside intact ones, and much of the industrial base keeps running through the fighting simply because no faction can afford to let it stop.
80.inhabitants: The population is dense and largely working, tied to the mills and assembly lines that keep the confederacy's factions all provisioned regardless of who currently holds a given block. Comfortable wages and steady work have not bought loyalty to any single council, and people tend to keep their politics private and their exits planned.  Long exposure to sudden fighting has made most residents unhurried in a crisis and quick to return to the machines once the shooting stops.

81.description: Veis produces the same modest goods it has produced for generations, its factory towns arranged in the same grid pattern the ruling council laid down long ago and never revised. The land itself offers little variation: flat, grey-skied basins given over to smelters and assembly sheds, with the same low hills repeating along every horizon. Nothing here has burned, flooded, or rebelled in living memory, and the official histories record this fact with evident satisfaction. It is a world that does exactly what is expected of it and nothing else.
81.inhabitants: The frogs of Veis work their shifts, file their production quotas, and go home, having long since learned that the council rewards steadiness and punishes anything resembling initiative. Comfortable enough to want little and watched closely enough to say less, they have made a quiet virtue of predictability.

82.description: Ensoreus packs its entire industrial output onto a small crust of land and reclaimed shelf, every district given over to refineries, assembly halls, and the corporate towers that own them. The world is small enough that its horizon curves close and its cities run into one another without gaps, forming a single continuous works broken only by transit rail and drainage canals. It is, by common agreement among those who have stopped here more than once, a tedious little planet: the weather is regulated, the shifts are fixed, and nothing on the surface varies from one district to the next.
82.inhabitants: The Black Fat Felines who staff Ensoreus's plants live under contracts issued by the corporate boards that hold title to the world, drawing steady wages and steady rations in exchange for steady, unremarkable labor. Wealth here is real but evenly administered, and the population has settled into a placid, well-fed routine that leaves little room for anything resembling incident.

83.description: Riveis spreads its farmland across a broad, gently rolling world, its holdings large enough that no single district dominates the others. Technology here remains simple, tools and transport kept plain and functional, yet scattered among the grain towns are the famed casino halls for which the world is known across the region. These houses, built up over generations from local timber and stone, draw gatherings from every settled corner despite the primitive means used to build and run them. Wealth is modest and evenly spread, the world getting by on steady harvests rather than surplus.
83.inhabitants: The native rodents that populate Riveis are mild-tempered and communal, organizing their scattered farm settlements through open democratic councils rather than any central authority. Long hours in the fields are balanced by evening gatherings at the gaming halls, which function as much as civic meeting places as houses of chance. Harmless by disposition, they prize fair dealing and open debate over ambition or accumulation.

84.description: Bivea's thin, patchy fields lie under skies prone to sudden flares that wash out radio chatter and scorch exposed crops without warning. Settlements are small and far apart, built low and half-buried where possible to escape the worst of the flare seasons. Farming here is a matter of guesswork and short growing windows, snatched between storms rather than planned around a calendar.
84.inhabitants: The Fierce Frogs who work this soil answer to no central authority, organizing locally and settling disputes among themselves as need arises. Generations of unpredictable skies have made them wary and self-reliant, quick to abandon a planting or a shelter the moment the light in the sky turns wrong.

85.description: Ermaso is a small world of thin soils and scattered clearings, its farmland carved out between stands of native timber rather than replacing it. Without any central authority to organize larger holdings, the scattered farmsteads work independently, trading among themselves for what the land will not give freely. The edible grub and the tree ant, both harvested from the surrounding woodland, form a staple of the diet across the settled clearings and are gathered as readily as anything sown in a field.
85.inhabitants: Households here answer to no wider law, settling disputes locally and relying on custom more than any written code. Life is hard and tools are simple, and most families divide their labor between meager crops and the steady work of gathering grubs and ants from the treeline. They are self-reliant people, wary of outsiders and unused to anyone claiming authority over their land.

86.description: Velete is given over to grain and root farms that spread across low, waterlogged plains, and the smell of fermenting mash and animal pens clings to every settlement large enough to have a name. Irrigation channels run alongside open drainage ditches, and the two are rarely kept apart, which accounts for much of the world's reputation. Modest processing works cluster near the larger towns, their runoff feeding straight back into the fields they draw from. Little here has been built with an eye to appearances; everything serves the harvest.
86.inhabitants: The elected councils that run each district spend most of their sessions arguing over water rights and grain quotas rather than sanitation, and little changes as a result. People here work long days in the mud for modest return, proud of their independence even as they complain, endlessly and to anyone who will listen, about the smell.

87.description: Engema's croplands ring a compact world given over almost entirely to cultivation, its holdings parceled and managed under corporate charter rather than by custom or clan. The soil is rich and the harvests reliable, but the world carries a sickness that moves through its settlements in slow, recurring waves, resisting every treatment the corporate clinics have tried. Quarantine districts stand alongside grain silos and processing plants, and travel between farming sectors is tightly controlled to slow the disease's spread. Even so, the fields are worked without pause, because the contracts that bind the population do not lapse for illness.
87.inhabitants: The black slimy lizards who work Engema's land answer to shareholders and estate managers rather than any local authority, their labor organized with the same efficiency applied to the harvest schedules and the sickness rosters. Comfortable wages and steady supply have kept discontent low, but the disease has bred a certain fatalism, a habit of working through symptoms rather than reporting them. They are practical, close-knit within their assigned sectors, and largely indifferent to matters outside the boundaries of their contracts.

88.description: Atrienxe crowds its factories and tenements across a small world with little room to spare, every district given over to smelting, fabrication or the housing needed to keep the workforce fed. The dictatorship that runs the place has never troubled itself with appearances, and the result is a colony of grey blocks, cracked pavement and industrial haze that most who pass through forget within a season. Nothing here was built to be looked at, only used, and it shows in every street.
88.inhabitants: The population works the mills and assembly lines in shifts set by the state, and steady wages have bought them a comfortable, unglamorous stability. They speak of their world without pride or complaint, the way people speak of a job they intend to keep doing until it is finished.

89.description: Beusrior packs a dense human population onto a small world whose factories run on advanced tooling but yield little worth shipping outward, a mismatch the local councils have long stopped apologizing for. The terrain is low and even, given over almost entirely to grey manufacturing blocks and the workers' quarters that ring them, with no coastline, range or ruin to break the monotony. Its reputation for dullness is not incidental but structural: uniform construction codes across the member-holds of the confederacy left every district looking much like the last.
89.inhabitants: The population lives well by any material measure, its wealth accumulated through generations of steady industrial output even as that output itself commands little interest beyond the system. Confederacy administration keeps labor and civic life tightly scheduled and evenly distributed, producing a people who are orderly, unhurried, and largely indifferent to novelty.

90.description: Ontiat is a large world of open farmland and modestly built market towns, spread thin across a landmass that has never been fully claimed. Its agricultural economy, ordinary in its crops and methods, is overshadowed by a persistent disease that moves through the population in slow, recurring waves and has shaped how the settlements are arranged, spaced, and quarantined from one another. Fields are worked in rotation with fallow zones left wider than farming alone would require, a precaution against contagion as much as soil exhaustion.
90.inhabitants: The Confederacy's scattered local councils manage outbreaks town by town, with little central authority to coordinate a unified response, so quarantine and care fall largely to the communities themselves. Colonials here are practical and wary, accustomed to sickness as a recurring cost of life rather than an emergency, and they measure neighbors by how reliably they help when a household is shut in.

91.description: Atarza is a small world given over to scattered industry, its few foundries and refineries built low and heavily shielded against solar activity that periodically floods the surface with radiation storms. There is no central authority to coordinate the work, so plants operate independently, cannibalizing failed neighbors for parts. The settlements sit far apart, each a self-contained cluster of furnaces and reinforced shelters rather than a proper town, with primitive tools compensating for what organization cannot provide.
91.inhabitants: Without government, the colonials rely on informal codes worked out between rival plant operators to keep the peace and share warning of incoming flares. Life here rewards those who can read the sky and shut down machinery before a storm hits, and poverty keeps most of the equipment patched together well past its intended use.

92.description: Arazaes is a broad, temperate world given over almost entirely to farmland and forest holdings, its low tech level suited to the steady rhythms of planting and harvest rather than industry. Vast tracts of woodland shelter the Arazaesian tree ant, whose mounds are a common sight along field boundaries, while ranchlands further out support the wolf herds bred for meat that has made the planet's name off-world. Settlements are spread thickly across the fertile lowlands, forming a patchwork of market towns rather than any single dominant city.
92.inhabitants: The population, descended from old colonial stock, governs itself through elected councils that manage land grants, herd quotas and the ant-harvest disputes that periodically flare between neighboring farms. Comfortable but unhurried, most Arazaesians take pride in working land their families have held for generations, and civic life revolves around the agricultural fairs where wolf meat and tree-ant produce are judged and traded.

93.description: Xeeranre is a small world of modest technology, its farmland broken by ranges where the mountain Quceoids are said to hunt, a curse older than any of the settlements that now avoid the higher slopes. Fields and orchards are worked in the lowland belts, with granaries and threshing yards clustered well clear of the foothills. The world has no single authority; each district answers to its own council or headman, and boundaries tend to follow the safe ground rather than any surveyed line.
93.inhabitants: The population, large furry insects organized into loose farming communities, keep to modest means and modest ambitions, tending crops enough to get by rather than to prosper. Generations of losses to the Quceoids have made them cautious planners, quick to abandon a good field if the mountain above it turns restless, and slow to trust any government that promises otherwise.

94.description: Quzadi is a sizeable world given over to industry, its skyline broken by refineries and fabrication yards that continue to operate even as the interior burns. Districts loyal to competing councils sit within sight of one another across ash-grey belts of ruined suburb, and freight lines are rerouted weekly to avoid whichever quarter has fallen this month. The official economy remains oddly comfortable on paper, propped up by state ledgers that have not caught up with the fighting. Development here means functioning power grids and working assembly lines standing next to bombed housing blocks that no one has been assigned to repair.
94.inhabitants: The furred, chitinous population is organized under committees and production quotas that persist out of habit even where the councils issuing them no longer agree on borders. Workers move between shifts and shelters with the same flat competence, having learned to treat factory discipline as the one constant left to them. Loyalty to the wider state has frayed into loyalty to a foreman, a block, a line supervisor who still shows up.

95.description: Isti is a large world of thin holdings and worn-out soil, its farmsteads spread far apart across long, weather-beaten plains. Manor estates hold what little wealth exists, and grain and root crops are worked by hand under primitive means with no machinery to spare. The world's one recreation of note is a Zero-G hockey league played in the vacuum sheds above the fields, a strange counterpoint to the plodding life below.
95.inhabitants: The colonials keep to themselves, wary of strangers and slow to speak, a shyness bred by generations of scattered holdings answering to distant lords. What community they have is found in the hockey sheds, where the same quiet families gather to watch or play, briefly loud among people otherwise given to silence.

96.description: Digebiti's vast landmass is broken by ranges the locals will not name aloud, where the phenomenon known only as the Xeoids stirs without warning and brings down slopes, rockfalls, and worse on any settlement built too near. Smelting works and ore towns cling instead to the lowland margins, their furnaces old and their output modest, feeding a feudal economy that never quite escapes want. Roads run in wide arcs around the high country, adding distance that the world's poverty can ill afford, and whole districts have been abandoned after a mountain moved.
96.inhabitants: The furred population lives under a patchwork of hereditary holdings, each lord answerable for the mines and forges within his reach and for keeping folk clear of the peaks. Generations of loss to the Xeoids have made them cautious and superstitious about high ground, quick to defer to any elder who claims to read the mountains' moods, and steady, unglamorous workers in the furnace towns where the real wealth of the world, such as it is, gets made.

97.description: Leoned is a small world under corporate charter, its farmland divided into leased plots that feed a population packed tightly across the stable ground between fault lines. Quakes come without warning and without pattern, and building codes across the settled belts favor low, braced structures over height. The Leonedian tree snake, prized in the terraria and exotic-pet trade of other worlds, breeds in the shelterbelts and orchard margins that separate the fields. Corporate surveyors have mapped the fault systems in detail, though the mapping has done little to make the tremors predictable.
97.inhabitants: The large black bug-eyed lizards who work Leoned's land do so under contracts issued by the agricultural combines that hold the leases, their days structured around planting quotas and quake drills in roughly equal measure. Comfortable wages and steady development have made them a settled, methodical people, unhurried in manner but quick to move when the ground starts to shift.

98.description: Enzaer's cramped landmass is given over almost entirely to production, with refineries and assembly complexes packed so close together that their runoff and smoke have fouled the air and the shallow seas alike. What passes for civic planning here is a dense lattice of factory blocks and worker tenements, laid out for output rather than comfort, and the result is widely regarded as squalid despite the wealth it generates. The dictatorship that runs Enzaer has never seen fit to spend its considerable industrial profits on cleaning the place up.
98.inhabitants: Human Colonials here work long shifts in the advanced production lines that make the world rich, while living amid grime and crowding that the ruling order treats as an acceptable cost of doing business. Loyalty to the state is assumed rather than earned, and most residents have learned to keep complaints about the filth to themselves.

99.description: Teraed's continents are given over almost entirely to refineries, foundries and assembly yards, each cluster answering to a different local administration with its own tariffs and codes. The result is a world without a unifying skyline or plan, just district after district of smoke-stained concrete under a permanent brown haze. Its wealth is real and its factories advanced, but nothing about the place has ever been built to look at, and no one has bothered fixing that.
99.inhabitants: The population works long shifts in plants owned by whichever authority holds the district that week, and most treat the constant turnover of local rule as background noise rather than politics. Colonials here are practical, unsentimental people, well paid but unimpressed by their own surroundings, and they tend to describe their home in the same flat terms outsiders use for it.

100.description: Vetitice's continents are given over almost entirely to refineries, distilleries and the tiered housing blocks that serve them, with little land left to anything but production. State-run stills along the equatorial belt turn out the brandy the world is famous for, a spirit strong enough that its export casks carry warning seals rather than vintage labels. In the capital's central districts stand the towering parking meters, ornate cast-iron relics of an earlier civic order that the planetary council maintains as monuments rather than instruments of use. Beyond these curiosities the world is one continuous industrial works, its skies grey with refinery haze from pole to pole.
100.inhabitants: Labour is organised through collective works councils, and most residents spend their working lives assigned to a single plant or distillery cooperative with little movement between trades. Wealth here is genuine but administered communally, so private fortune shows itself less in property than in ration allotments of the brandy itself, prized and carefully rationed even among those who make it.

101.description: Laenin's collective farms spread thin across rolling grain country, their fields worked by hand under a government that owns every harvest before it is cut. The disease that moves through its villages in slow waves has left whole hamlets shuttered and its clinics permanently overwhelmed, a burden the planet's primitive medicine cannot lift. Older still than the sickness is the colony's hostility toward broadcast comedy, a grudge folded into local law and enforced with the same seriousness given to grain quotas.
101.inhabitants: Laenin's people are farmers first, organized into work brigades that answer to distant planners rather than to each other. Generations of loss to the recurring sickness have made them fatalistic and close-mouthed, and their long-standing contempt for televised sit coms is treated less as taste than as a matter of communal honor.

102.description: Beraanxe is a small world whose land is broken into scattered holdings, each answering to its own local authority rather than any central rule. Its oceans run strange colours and thicker currents than most worlds, folding and shimmering under low light in ways that draw comment from every visiting captain. Farms cling to the coastal shelves between these tidal bands, working plots of shallow soil with tools that owe nothing to modern industry. Settlements are few and far between, and what wealth exists comes slowly, from the soil and the sea rather than from any factory.
102.inhabitants: The Black Slimy Lobsters that hold this world divide themselves among many small governments, yet share a rare warmth toward outsiders that outweighs their political differences. Life on modest farms and fisheries keeps most occupied with plain, steady labour, but hospitality toward those from off-world is treated almost as a civic duty. Their fondness for visitors has become as much a mark of the place as the strange waters they fish.'

103.description: Atage offers little to distinguish it from a hundred other small industrial worlds under central rule. Its factories and processing yards cover much of the habitable crust, feeding a populace packed into tiered residential blocks around each production zone. Nothing in its geography, climate or history has given it a reputation beyond that of a competent, forgettable producer.
103.inhabitants: The population works to quotas set from above, and the dictatorship's planners favour steady output over any particular specialism, which suits a people who have grown used to comfortable, unremarkable lives. Colonial stock through and through, they take a quiet pride in reliability rather than ambition.

104.description: Veisti's surface is given over almost entirely to industry, its cities organized in tight concentric rings around processing complexes that never go dark. Between the manufacturing districts, corporate housing towers rise in uniform blocks, broken here and there by the vast domed arenas built for zero-gravity cricket, the planet's chief export of culture rather than goods. The atmosphere above the factory belts carries a permanent haze, scrubbed at intervals by municipal systems paid for out of corporate revenue rather than public funds.
104.inhabitants: Employment here is arranged almost entirely through the controlling corporations, and life follows their shift patterns and their architecture down to the color of the uniforms. Off the factory floor the population is notably withdrawn, preferring correspondence and scheduled meetings to unstructured company, an eccentric shyness at odds with the roaring crowds who fill the domed arenas whenever a cricket match is called.

105.description: Zaerla is a small, thinly settled world whose economy runs on subsistence farming under the authority of local feudal lords. Its holdings are scattered and self-contained, each managing its own fields and livestock pens with little contact beyond the nearest boundary stone. What reputation the world carries beyond its own sky rests on its exotic cuisine, built almost entirely around the large black fat birds that dominate its farmyards and its tables.
105.inhabitants: The people are farmers and herders bound to their lord's land, working with primitive tools and old methods passed down through generations. Rearing and preparing the black fat birds is both livelihood and craft, a skill regarded with more pride than the poverty of the manor otherwise allows.

106.description: Esredice is a sizeable world of grey industrial townships strung along low ridgelines, each producing whatever the local lord's manufactories can wring from thin ore seams and tired soil. Nothing marks its history with distinction: no war, no disaster, no invention has given it a name beyond its own. The sky is flat and pale most of the year, and the works below run on the same schedules they always have. Visiting officials of the merchant guilds have described its ledgers as the least remarkable in the sector, and left it at that.
106.inhabitants: The people work the foundries and workshops their fief-holders assign them and expect little else from the arrangement. Under the local lords, ambition is a quiet, private matter, rarely spoken of and never encouraged; life proceeds at the same even pace it has for generations, and most colonials seem content, or resigned, to let it.

107.description: Beor is a small world of collective farms and irrigation cooperatives, its low hills terraced into grain plots and orchard rows under a modest technical base. Nothing distinguishes its towns from one another; the same prefabricated grain silos and communal halls repeat across every district. Despite the fertility of its soil, the place has earned a reputation as an unremarkable dump, a world visited for its produce and forgotten as soon as the holds are full.
107.inhabitants: The colonials work assigned plots under collective directives, their days measured by harvest quotas rather than personal ambition. Life is plain and communal, without much complaint but without much hope of change, and the people carry a resigned, workmanlike pride in soil that yields more than the system around them ever gives back.

108.description: Orso is a sizeable world given over largely to mixed industry, its skyline broken by broadcast towers rather than any single dominant structure. Studio districts sprawl across several administrative zones, each run under its own local charter, producing the sit coms for which the world is reasonably fabled. Manufacturing quarters nearby turn out household goods for domestic markets, chief among them the food blenders that have become something of a civic obsession.
108.inhabitants: The population lives under a patchwork of overlapping local governments, each jealous of its own studio contracts and factory output, which gives daily life a competitive, parochial flavour despite the shared culture. Comfortable wages and steady industrial work leave people with leisure enough to follow the broadcasts closely and to argue, with real passion, over the merits of one blender model against another.

109.description: Usatqura is a broad world of thin soils and unpredictable rain, given over almost entirely to grain and root farming worked with hand tools and draft animals. Its farmsteads and market towns spread across the lowlands without much central planning, each cluster of holdings tending to its own affairs. The planet has acquired a certain notoriety for the sheer intensity with which its people despise broadcast situation comedies, a subject on which they will hold forth at length and without prompting.
109.inhabitants: The colonials govern themselves through town meetings and elected councils, a habit that suits a population used to arguing everything out before acting on it. Life is modest and the work is steady rather than rewarding, which leaves little patience for entertainment that treats hardship as a joke, and a great deal of patience for saying so.

110.description: Erbiti's landmass is given over almost entirely to great dense forests, broken only by the low sprawl of processing camps and rusting mills that pass for industry here. What manufacturing exists clings to the timber trade, sawmills and pulping sheds strung along cleared river corridors, their output modest and their machinery old. No central authority manages the forests or the settlements within them, and the boundaries between one logging claim and the next are settled by those strong enough to hold them.
110.inhabitants: The large felines who work these forests are scattered thin across the world, living in small logging camps and mill towns with no government above the camp itself. Poverty and the absence of law have made them self-reliant and wary of outsiders, quick to settle disputes over timber rights and water access without appeal to anyone but themselves.

111.description: Reinen presents itself as a vast plain of grain and root fields, broken at regular intervals by identical processing towns laid out on the same grid pattern from one horizon to the next. The world's size means the fields go on for a very long journey in any direction, and the sameness of the terrain has become the planet's defining feature rather than any hazard or wonder. Confederacy administrators rotate through the agricultural districts on fixed schedules, and little in the way of local event disturbs the routine of planting, harvest and shipment.
111.inhabitants: The Black Bug-Eyed Lobsters who work the fields and cooperatives favor consensus and procedure, a habit reinforced by decades of confederate committee rule and steady, unspectacular yields. Comfortable but unexcitable, they speak of the work in the same even tone they use for the weather, and visitors are given the same tour every season because there is, by common agreement, nothing else to show.

112.description: Ininbi is a large world of aging factory belts and worked-over terrain, its horizon broken by refineries and processing towers that long ago outpaced the ground's capacity to support them cleanly. The economy remains poor by the standards of its advanced technology, a mismatch that shows in patched infrastructure kept running past its intended span. Settlements sit dense and close along the industrial corridors, built for output rather than comfort. Gambling houses have been tried here more than once and each has failed or been driven out, a fact locals mention with some satisfaction.
112.inhabitants: The insect population organizes itself through a confederacy of semi-autonomous hive-districts, each managing its own labor and output while deferring to shared councils on larger matters. Generations of industrial toil under that arrangement have produced a temperament that values steady, visible return on effort and holds games of chance in open contempt, seeing them as a mockery of the collective labor that built the world. Wealth here is measured in production and reserves, not in stakes won or lost.

113.description: Erlaza is a small world of worn, ancient mountains that fold down into modest farmland, the ranges themselves scoured smooth by ages of wind rather than any recent violence. Its agricultural holdings, mostly grain and root crops worked from scattered lowland villages, sustain the colony without much surplus. The land carries a lethal disease that surfaces in waves, and quarantine notices posted at the edges of settlements are as common a sight as harvest markers.
113.inhabitants: The colonials live under a dictatorship that keeps close account of who moves where, largely in the name of containing the sickness that shadows the population. Farmers and quarantine wardens work in uneasy partnership, and a wary, watchful manner has become the ordinary way of greeting strangers and neighbors alike.

114.description: Celabile's temperate lowlands are given over almost entirely to combine-run plantations, their fields divided by dead-straight service roads and orbital relay towers rather than fences. The corporate estates that own this land have poured wealth into pressurised arenas where zero-gravity hockey is played before packed galleries, a sport bred here and nowhere else. The world's other claim to fame is stranger: a poet, long dead, whose verses are so bleak and cutting that they are still quoted, half in horror and half in admiration, across every canteen and boardroom on the planet.
114.inhabitants: Most residents work under contract to the agricultural combines that administer the planet, their lives structured by company housing, company schedules, and company loyalty oaths. Off duty they follow hockey league standings with fierce partisanship and recite the poet's grimmer lines with a kind of proud unease, as if the verses explain something about themselves they would rather not say outright.

115.description: Ribiso is a broad, gently curved world given over almost entirely to grain and tuber farms that spread across its lowland basins in long unbroken strips. Its towns are modest and widely spaced, each built around a grain silo and, more often than not, a sealed arena where the local passion is played out. That passion is vacuum cricket, contested inside airless domes raised on the edges of the farmland, where the ball travels true and the players work in suits built for the harvest as much as the pitch. The world's wealth is thin and evenly spread, its people content to work the fields and fill the stands rather than chase anything grander.
115.inhabitants: Ribiso's colonials are farmers first, voting their own town councils and cooperative boards with the same plain seriousness they bring to tending crops. Modest tools and modest means keep ambitions local, and the vacuum cricket leagues give the scattered farming communities their one great shared excitement, argued over in market halls long after the matches end.

116.description: Qudira is a wide and thinly peopled world, its cleared farmland separated by long stretches of scrub and forest left to itself. Among the trees grow the talking treeoids, gnarled and slow, whose reputation for cursing at passers-by has outlasted any explanation of how it started. What little surplus the farms yield goes into the fermenting vats that produce the Leveti gargle blaster, a drink brewed and argued over in equal measure across the scattered holdings. There is no capital to speak of, only farmsteads and hamlets that answer to no one but themselves.
116.inhabitants: Without any central authority, the Qudirans organize around family plots and loose local custom, settling disputes among themselves as they arise. Farming with old tools and older methods, they are patient, self-reliant, and unbothered by the treeoids' insults, which most regard as background noise rather than provocation.

117.description: Isdibi spreads across broad forested lowlands and river floodplains, most of it left to grow wild for want of hands to clear it. What farms exist cling to burned clearings and riverbanks, hedged against the tree canopy that presses in on every side. The colony's grim distinction is the tree ant, a biting swarm-insect whose nests riddle the woodland and whose venom has closed off entire districts of otherwise arable ground.
117.inhabitants: Without any central authority, the scattered farmsteads answer only to themselves, trading news and warnings of fresh ant swarms along footpaths rather than roads. Life here favors the wary and the self-reliant, and families measure a season's success as much by which fields stayed clear of the ants as by the size of the harvest.

118.description: Gequre is a small agricultural world whose modest patchwork of farms and pasture has been broken and burned in stretches by ongoing civil war. Its settlements sit at a moderate density across the arable land, many now scarred or half-abandoned, and the fields that survive are worked with tools scarcely advanced beyond hand and beast. The world's one point of regional fame is the Gequrian tree ant, studied and traded in small quantities even as the fighting continues around the groves where it lives.
118.inhabitants: The colonials hold to their democratic institutions more out of habit and stubbornness than confidence, voting in townships that may change hands between factions from one season to the next. Life is hard and getting by is the general condition, with farmers and militia often drawn from the same families, and a wary, practical resilience marks most dealings with strangers and neighbors alike.

119.description: Rarere's arable belts wrap the temperate latitudes in orderly grids, each parcel leased from the holding company that administers the world's soil, water rights and distilleries alike. Beyond the brandy for which it is mildly known, the planet turns most of its harvest into feed grain and pressed oils shipped out under corporate seal. Towns cluster at rail junctions between the estates, built to a uniform plan that leaves little room for anything not sanctioned by the company charter.
119.inhabitants: Most residents work land they do not own, drawing steady wages and company housing in exchange for loyalty to the ledger. Generations of tending the same fields have given them a quiet, practical pride in the brandy that carries the world's name off-planet, even as the profits from it settle mostly in boardrooms above their heads.

120.description: Aerater spreads wide and empty, its farms scattered thin across a surface too large for the hands available to work it. Crops grow in a haze of rot and standing water, and the settlements that dot the lowlands smell of the compost heaps and animal pens that surround them. The world has earned its poor reputation honestly: irrigation ditches run foul, waste is left where it falls, and the air itself carries the smell for kilometers before any building comes into view. Little has been done to fix this, since little here is done for any reason but survival.
120.inhabitants: The colonials work the land under a dictatorship that extracts what it can and reinvests nothing, leaving farms primitive and families spread thin across the wilderness. They are hard, unsentimental people, used to filth and short rations, who measure a season only by whether the harvest was enough to avoid the ruler's punishment for shortfall.

121.description: Atbevete is a small world given over almost entirely to industry, its cities packed close along whatever level ground the terrain allows. Distilleries and blending halls dominate the skyline, and the planet's name is attached, mildly but persistently, to the Le gargle blaster, a drink notorious well beyond its own confederacy. The settlements have grown dense and vertical rather than wide, a consequence of holding a large population on limited land.
121.inhabitants: The people of Atbevete work in shifts that keep the distilleries running near constantly, and the wealth generated flows back into close, crowded neighbourhoods rather than open estates. Governed as a confederacy of allied districts, they take a certain pride in local production and in the reputation, however dubious, that their signature export has earned them off-world.

122.description: Bioris is a world of rolling farmland and scattered market towns, its economy built on grain, root crops and pasture rather than any single great estate. Fields are worked with simple tools and animal traction, and the settlements remain small and spread thin across the arable belts. The world's renown rests almost entirely on the Biorisian edible poet, a delicacy raised and prepared with methods that have not changed across generations and that no other world has managed to reproduce. Beyond that trade the planet is otherwise unremarkable, a quiet agricultural confederation getting by on modest yields.
122.inhabitants: The people of Bioris are farmers and smallholders organized into a loose confederacy of townships, each holding its own council and its own claim to a share of the poet harvest. Life here is plain and communal, shaped by shared labor and shared scarcity rather than any central authority, and pride in the local delicacy runs deeper than any political loyalty.

123.description: Raale is a thinly populated world of modest size, its fields worked by hand between scattered hamlets that owe no allegiance to any central rule. The land yields little beyond subsistence crops, and what surplus exists is bartered rather than sold through any formal market. Its one renown is the Raalian edible poet, a strange cultivated organism prized off-world for its taste and named, so the story goes, for the way it seems to compose itself into shapes as it grows. Roads are few, and most trade between hamlets moves along footpaths and cart tracks worn over generations.
123.inhabitants: The colonials of Raale answer to no government beyond custom and the authority of whichever elder a hamlet trusts, and disputes are settled locally rather than referred elsewhere. Life is hard and tools are simple, so most hands are given over to growing food or tending the poet-beds that bring the world its only fame. Strangers are met with the wary courtesy of people who have little to spare and long memories of those who have taken it anyway.

124.description: Tionisla's industrial estates spread across its temperate lowlands in orderly blocks, feeding an economy built on steady manufacturing rather than speculative trade. The cities are laid out with wide buffers between residential quarters and public plazas, a planning choice that long predates the current administration but suits it well. Its wealth is evident in the upkeep of infrastructure rather than in display, and the world carries an air of quiet, functioning order.
124.inhabitants: The lizard population is famed across the region for a deep-set reticence, conducting business through intermediaries and written correspondence where other worlds would default to face-to-face dealing. Public assemblies under the democratic government tend toward long silences and careful, minimal statements rather than open debate. Even so, the industrial output of the world speaks to a workforce that is disciplined and exacting, however little it says for itself.

125.description: Encereso is a small world of rich soil and fractured rule, its fertile valleys divided among rival governments that hold no border for long. Orchards and grain terraces stretch across the lowlands, tended between raids and left to rot when the fighting shifts. Villages are few and far between, scattered rather than clustered, each one loyal to whichever faction last passed through with weapons. The land gives generously; the people who work it rarely keep what it gives.
125.inhabitants: The lizard clans who work Encereso's fields are farmers first and soldiers by necessity, their tools doubling as arms when a rival warband crosses the treeline. Wealth here is measured in stored grain rather than coin, and what little surplus exists is buried, hidden, or burned rather than surrendered. Generations of civil war have left them wary of strangers and stranger still of their own neighbors.

126.description: Anerbe's continents are cut by ranges of active volcanoes, their slopes terraced with grain and root fields worked by cooperative brigades. The land is broad enough that farm collectives spread across whole provinces, each feeding into regional depots under the direction of central planning committees. What draws most outside notice, though, are the domed arenas built near the calderas, where vacuum karate is practiced in sight of the smoking peaks, a pairing of danger and ceremony the world is widely known for.
126.inhabitants: The population, dominated by placid, feathered bird-like people, organizes its labor around collective quotas and shared harvests, with volcanic ash enriching fields that keep most households modestly fed rather than prosperous. Their tolerance for risk shows less in daily farm work than in their enthusiasm for the karate bouts, which the state stages as public spectacle and civic pride alike.

127.description: Gelaed is a small world whose fertile lowlands are given over almost entirely to the pink-leaved Edla Beweed, grown in terraced plantations that ring the industrial townships. Refineries and processing works cluster near the fields, drawing on plantation labor to turn the crop into export stock, though the smoke of factory districts often mixes with that of burned holdings. The countryside is scarred in patches by fighting between rival estates, with fences, fields and roads rebuilt and broken again as fortunes shift. Settlements are dense and close-packed, built for defense as much as for trade.
127.inhabitants: Power on Gelaed rests with landed lords whose private levies fight for control of plantation ground, and most people owe labor or loyalty to one estate or another. Life is organized around the Beweed harvest and the factories that process it, but plans are made with the expectation that war may interrupt them, and most families keep half an eye on the horizon for smoke. Wealth is modest and unevenly held, and the population is used to getting by rather than getting ahead.”

128.description: Onusorle spreads across a large landmass of thin industrial belts strung between the holdings of local lords, its factories old and its ore veins nearly worked out. What wealth remains comes from small stills and hunting grounds rather than the furnaces, and the world is mildly well known beyond its own sky for its vicious brew and its wolf cutlet, both born of necessity turned to habit. Settlement is thin and scattered, clusters of workshops and smokestacks holding to the edges of each lord's domain.
128.inhabitants: The Black Bug-Eyed Birds who work the Onusorlian belts owe labor and loyalty upward through a chain of feudal holders, and little of the industrial output ever leaves the estate that claims it. Life is hard but not desperate, and much of what pride remains is invested in the brew-houses and hunting lodges that produce the world's small fame, rather than in the failing mills.

129.description: Zaonce presents flat continents of processing plants and residential blocks arranged with corporate efficiency, the horizon broken by identical rows of manufacturing towers. Its climate is temperate and unremarkable, its cities laid out on grids that repeat from one district to the next without variation. The advanced industrial economy runs smoothly and without incident, producing goods in steady volume, and little else of note ever happens here.
129.inhabitants: The population, fierce harmless slimy rodents, works long shifts within the corporate structure that owns most of the world outright, moving between shift and quarters in patterns as fixed as the architecture. Wealth here is considerable but evenly administered, and the inhabitants show little inclination toward anything beyond the routines their employer has set for them.

130.description: Diquer is a large world given over almost entirely to farmland, its horizon broken only by grain silos and the low ridgelines that separate one holding from the next. Settlements are few and far between, each one a cluster of packed-earth roads and timber storehouses serving the estates around it. Little of note ever happens here; the seasons turn, the crops come in, and the same quiet repeats itself across the plains.
130.inhabitants: The colonials who work Diquer's fields answer to a single ruling authority that sets quotas and takes its share before anything reaches storage. Life is steady rather than hard, and people speak of their days in terms of planting and harvest rather than ambition. Visitors from elsewhere are rare enough that most families have never had reason to expect one.

131.description: Zadies turns beneath restless flares that strip its upper atmosphere and bathe its cities in surges of static and radiation warning klaxons. Its industrial belts run underground or beneath radiation-hardened domes, where factory lines press out kitchenware and small appliances for export across neighbouring jurisdictions. No single authority governs the world; overlapping charters and rival administrations divide the industrial zones, each fiercely protective of its own production quotas. Among the countless goods stamped out in its foundries, the food blender holds a curious cultural primacy, appearing in shopfronts, shrines, and civic emblems alike.
131.inhabitants: The native rodents, wiry and thick-hided against solar glare, work the shielded factory floors with a territorial snarl that outsiders mistake for hostility but locals recognize as ordinary temperament. Comfortable wages and steady industrial demand have made them proud of their craft, and nowhere is that pride sharper than in the endless competing designs of blenders turned out under each district's separate banner. Loyalty runs to district and foundry long before it runs to any planetary idea, and disputes over blender patents are argued with the same ferocity as territorial ones.

132.description: Entizadi turns beneath a star given to violent flares, and its cities are built low and shielded, with radiation-hardened domes clustered along shadowed valleys where the worst of the surges cannot reach. State-run manufacturing lines occupy much of the crust's usable surface, producing goods for a population packed tightly across a small landmass. Among the endless output of the collective foundries, the small kitchen appliance holds a strange, disproportionate status, appearing in shrines, murals, and workers' council emblems alike.
132.inhabitants: The Horned Birds work their assigned shifts in vast cooperative factories, their lives organized around production quotas and shelter drills timed to solar forecasts. Off duty, they gather in communal kitchens where the shared blending of food into elaborate pastes and foams is treated less as chore than as art form and quiet act of civic pride.

133.description: Esanbe's continents sit astride active fault lines, and the tremors that roll through its farm belts are frequent enough to have shaped how the world builds and plants. Fields are laid out in wide, low terraces rather than tall structures, and grain silos are reinforced against collapse rather than built for height. The world produces most of what it eats and exports the surplus through a handful of collective distribution centers rather than open markets. Public sentiment against games of chance runs deep here, old enough that no settlement, however small, has ever permitted a casino to open.
133.inhabitants: Esanbe's colonials work state-organized farms and cooperatives, their days shaped as much by seismic drills as by harvest schedules. Wealth is shared modestly but reliably, and the communal temperament that built collective granaries also sustains an unbending, almost puritanical scorn for gambling in any form.

134.description: Usralaat's crust is restless, cut by fault lines that run beneath its scattered industrial districts and shake loose whole rows of prefabricated housing without warning. Foundries and refineries are built low and braced heavy, favoured over height for the simple reason that tall structures do not survive long here. Settlement remains sparse across the sizeable landmass, with communities strung along the more stable ridgelines rather than the fertile but treacherous lowlands.
134.inhabitants: The various regional authorities that share governance rarely agree on much beyond building codes, which are strict and unevenly enforced. Workers rotate through shift patterns designed around seismic monitoring rather than daylight, and most households keep a bag packed near the door out of long habit rather than instruction. Getting by is the general condition, and the colonials speak of the ground itself the way other worlds speak of weather.

135.description: Anlere is a sizeable world of good soil and steady rain, its lowlands given over almost entirely to grain and orchard holdings that answer to the state. Settlement follows the river valleys and the coastal plains, where the larger estates cluster around processing depots built to modest specification. The world's small spotted shrew is noted in trade circulars and naturalist logs alike, though the woodlands beyond the cultivated belt harbor tree leopards whose raids on livestock and outlying farmsteads are a persistent and unresolved trouble.
135.inhabitants: Farm labor here is organized under central direction, with quotas set from the capital and little room for independent enterprise. Most colonials work the land or the depots that process it, getting by on wages fixed well below what the harvests are worth, and those posted to the outer farmsteads keep watch for leopards as a matter of routine rather than alarm.

136.description: Teveri is a large world given over almost entirely to agriculture, its plains divided into vast leased holdings that answer to the corporate boards holding title to them. Among its exports the fermented crop drink known locally as evil juice has earned a name for itself well beyond the system, brewed in cooperative distilleries attached to the larger farm combines. Settlement is dense for a world of its kind, with grain towns and processing depots strung close together along the main rail lines rather than scattered.
136.inhabitants: The population works under contract to the companies that own the land beneath them, comfortable in provision but bound closely to schedules set from the corporate offices in the capital. Teverians have a reputation, well earned, for a reticence bordering on shyness, a quiet that shows in short transactions and long silences at the edges of the grain towns.

137.description: Sotiera's farmland spreads across terraced valleys beneath ranges that shift without warning, and the tremors have shaped everything from field boundaries to the low, squat halls of its manors. Villages sit apart from one another along fault lines, rebuilt more than once, their granaries and shrines reinforced against the next collapse. The world's name travels further than its goods ever do, carried by verses attributed to a solitary mountain poet whose lines are recited in halls far from where they were written. Beyond that reputation, Sotiera remains a quiet, hard-worked place of terraced grain and thin harvests.
137.inhabitants: Bound to their lords by custom rather than law, the farmers of Sotiera work land they do not own and rebuild what the ground periodically takes from them. Generations of loss have made them practical and unsentimental about property, though the poet's verses are kept and repeated as something the earthquakes cannot claim.

138.description: Ededleen's industrial belts sprawl beneath a haze of manufacturing smoke, their furnaces and foundries feeding a population that has long since outgrown the fields around it. The soil is thin and the mines are older than memory, so the world has turned instead to its kitchens, where spiced river-fish, fermented root mash and roasted insect-meat dishes have become something of a local art. Great feudal households compete as much over table settings and rare ingredients as over land or ore rights, and market districts near the refineries double as open-air kitchens through the dinner hours.
138.inhabitants: Loyalty runs upward through households and guild-kitchens rather than through any central authority, and status is measured as much in recipes guarded and passed down as in land held. Laborers in the foundries and refineries eat well despite the grime of their trade, and the great houses that hold nominal rule over them compete for renown by hosting feasts that draw talk from beyond the world itself.

139.description: Inonri's continents are broken by volcanic fields whose calderas vent gas in slow, colour-changing plumes rather than the usual smoke and ash, a phenomenon that draws study teams from beyond the system and gives the world its odd renown. Between the fields, collectivised ranches breed the native wolf stock whose meat has become the planet's signature export, processed and packed in state combines near the volcanic belt for the mineral-rich grazing it affords. Industrial districts ring the calmer lowlands, turning out manufactured goods on a scale that keeps the whole large world employed and well provisioned. Housing blocks and factory halls spread across the settled land in dense, planned rows, a pattern repeated from one province to the next.
139.inhabitants: Labour on Inonri is organised through state ranching and manufacturing collectives, and most residents spend their working lives within one or the other. Generations of steady industrial wages under a planned economy have made the population comfortable and disciplined, proud of the wolf herds and the strange fire-mountains that outsiders travel to see.

140.description: Esbeus is a sizeable world of worn, ancient mountain chains that fold across its continents, softened by age but still restless underfoot. Frequent earthquakes shake the settled valleys and terraced farmland below, cracking irrigation channels and toppling the older stone buildings faster than they can be rebuilt. Farming towns are spread thinly along the more stable lowlands, each cluster of holdings answering to its own local charter rather than any single authority over the world. The soil remains fertile despite the tremors, and agriculture continues much as it always has, patched together after every fresh collapse.
140.inhabitants: The scattered local governments leave each district to manage its own quakes, debts and harvests, and colonials here have grown practical and unsentimental about rebuilding what falls. Modest tools and poor returns keep most families working the same land for generations, mending walls and terraces as often as tending crops.

141.description: Lerelace is a small world given over almost entirely to manufacturing, its landmass divided into close-packed industrial districts linked by elevated transit ways. The factories run in continuous shifts, producing the refined goods that have made the planet wealthy, and little else about the place invites comment. Housing blocks and processing plants repeat across the horizon in the same grey pattern, and the world's reputation for tedium is well earned by design as much as by accident.
141.inhabitants: The colonials who work these lines are prosperous under their elected councils, and the democracy they maintain runs with the same steady efficiency as the plants that employ most of the population. Life here rewards competence and punctuality over ambition, and most residents seem content to let the factories define the rhythm of their days.

142.description: Eszaraxe spreads its thin farms and pastures across a wide, mountainous landmass, with settlement thinning out to almost nothing across the high ranges. The soil supports little beyond hardy grain and grazing stock, and the planet's fame rests on two unlikely exports: the spotted shrew that burrows through its upland scree, and the tradition of verse composed by herders and hill-dwellers who have made poetry out of isolation. No central authority manages the land or its people, and settlements exist as scattered, self-governing clusters separated by empty country.
142.inhabitants: The colonials live thinly across the mountains and lowlands, working small holdings with tools that owe more to necessity than design. Without government to arbitrate disputes or organise labour, most matters are settled within family and clan, and the same silence that shapes their poetry shapes their dealings with strangers.

143.description: Anbeen's landmass is dominated by great tropical forests, their canopies broken only by river deltas and the terraced clearings of agricultural settlement. The world's fortune is undercut by dreadful solar activity, storms of radiation that scour the upper atmosphere and play havoc with orbital and surface instruments alike. Farming communities have adapted by building beneath the forest canopy itself, using the dense growth as a natural shield against the worst of the flares. Despite this, the forests remain the world's defining wealth, yielding produce enough to support a sizeable and comfortable population.
143.inhabitants: The Black Frogs of Anbeen govern themselves as a confederacy of forest-district councils, each responsible for its own stretch of canopy and cropland, coordinating only when solar activity threatens shared infrastructure. Generations of living with the flares have made them methodical and unhurried, more concerned with resilience than speed, and their developed technology is applied chiefly to shielding, storage and the steady business of growing food under difficult skies.'

144.description: Biorle's surface is given over almost entirely to manufacturing districts, laid out in the same grey grid pattern from one horizon to the other, broken only by connecting rail and the low ridgelines the builders did not bother to level. The world's industry has long since passed its productive peak, leaving factory stacks that still run but produce little worth noting, and the atmosphere carries a permanent haze of exhaust that dulls the light at all hours. Nothing here is scenic, dangerous, or unusual, a fact the local almanacs record with the same flatness they would use for anything else. Biorle is, by common agreement among those who have seen it and those who have not, simply dull.
144.inhabitants: The population lives in dense residential blocks attached directly to the factories that employ them, under a confederate administration more concerned with balancing member interests than improving the view. Wealth here sits oddly against the tired industrial base, most of it held in finance and service concerns that have grown up alongside the aging plants rather than from them. People are civil, unhurried, and largely indifferent to the world's reputation, having long since stopped expecting Biorle to be anything other than what it is.

145.description: Anisor's continents are given over to mixed industrial zones, their factory districts arranged in concentric rings around older municipal cores that predate the current order. Gambling houses are banned outright across the planet, a policy that traces back to customs older than the dictatorship itself and enforced with more consistency than most of its other laws. Courtship on Anisor follows rites that have outlasted several changes of government, observed in public squares and factory towns alike, and the planet's reputation rests as much on these as on anything it manufactures.
145.inhabitants: The population works largely in industry, organized under a firm central authority that leaves little room for dissent but keeps most households comfortable. Off the factory floor, life still runs on inherited custom: elaborate courtship rituals are treated as public business rather than private matter, and any mention of casinos or wagering draws open, unembarrassed contempt.

146.description: Usrarema's industrial belts wrap the temperate lowlands in refinery smoke and cultivation domes, feeding an advanced manufacturing base that dominates the local economy. The world is heavily populated, its cities built dense and vertical around corporate headquarters that manage both production and land. It owes its reputation less to any machine than to the Usraremaian edible poet, a cultivated organism raised in shaded terrace farms and prized across the settled worlds as both delicacy and curiosity.
146.inhabitants: The small black slimy rodents native to Usrarema hold every level of the corporate hierarchy, from terrace cultivators tending the edible poet crops to executives overseeing the industrial concerns that own the planet outright. Wealth here is concentrated but widely felt, and the rodents carry themselves with the brisk, contractual manner of a people for whom employment and citizenship are the same document.

147.description: Diso is a large world given over to broad agricultural belts, its most storied feature being the Ti corn plantations that have worked the same soils for generations. These fields, laid out in long terraces to catch the light, remain the world's quiet claim to fame beyond its own borders. Frequent solar activity disrupts communications and casts long static-laced afternoons over the growing regions, a hazard the planet has learned to schedule around rather than solve.
147.inhabitants: The Black Furry Feline population lives well by the standards of an agricultural world, its democratic institutions favoring cooperative management of the plantations and steady reinvestment in local infrastructure. Generations of dealing with solar interference have made them practical about timing and communication, favoring redundancy over urgency in most of their affairs.

148.description: Riraes turns a wide face of pink ocean toward space, the colour said to come from mineral salts and microbial blooms that never quite settle. Along its shorelines and inland basins, wind and old volcanic action have carved rock into leaning spires and hollowed arches that draw comparison from every crew that overflies them. The industry here is old and undercapitalised, scattered foundries and refineries working the mineral wealth of the stone country without much coordination or investment. Settlements sit apart from one another, strung along the coasts where the water is workable and the ground is stable.
148.inhabitants: The rodent population governs itself through no single authority, and local works crews, foundry gangs and coastal communities strike their own bargains and settle their own disputes. Money is short and machinery older than most of the people running it, so life leans on improvisation, barter, and a hard-won knack for keeping worn equipment functional. Independence is prized more than comfort, and outsiders find little patience for anyone claiming to speak for the whole world.

149.description: Orrira is a sizeable world of scattered forges and smoke-blackened valleys, its industry crude and hand-built rather than mechanized in any organized sense. Great stands of treeoids cover much of the lowland terrain, plants that speak in low murmurs to any who pass near and are said to kill before they can be eaten, though the locals eat them regardless. No central authority coordinates the smelting camps or the logging of the treeoid groves, and settlements remain few, spread wide across the wilderness between one furnace town and the next.
149.inhabitants: The furred, feline population lives in loose clan holdings built around ore pits and charcoal kilns, each answerable to no one beyond its own foremen and elders. Poverty and the absence of law have made them practical and wary, quick to abandon a claim when the treeoids nearby turn restless, and quicker still to defend a working furnace with tooth and blade.

150.description: Xeer is a small world whose farmland has been given over almost entirely to livestock ranging, with paddocks and feed lots ringing every settlement of note. The wolf herds that give the world its name graze the upland pasture beyond the towns, and the meat trade built around them has shaped the layout of the markets, smokehouses and dining halls that anchor the larger settlements. Restaurants and communal kitchens crowd the town centres, and much of the built environment seems arranged around the serving of food rather than its production.
150.inhabitants: The population lives well by the standards of a farming world, and the comfortable wealth spread through its democratic institutions shows in the care taken over cooking, plating and the running of kitchens as skilled trades in their own right. Ranchers, butchers and chefs hold comparable standing here, and civic argument runs as often to recipes and grazing rights as to policy.

151.description: Ceesxe's continents are given over almost entirely to rain forest, a green cover so extensive that its refineries and processing plants are threaded through the canopy rather than cut against it. Corporate holdings claim entire watersheds, running pipelines and transit cables between forest-floor extraction sites and the tower complexes that rise above the treeline. The world's wealth is built on what the forest yields, and little of the original ground cover remains untouched by some concession or another.
151.inhabitants: Fierce Bony Birds dominate the corporate hierarchies here, their sharp tempers well suited to boardrooms run like territorial disputes. Labor and management alike answer to the holding companies that carved up the forest generations back, and status is measured in the size of one's concession rather than any older mark of rank.

152.description: Isatre spreads across flat, gray plains given over almost entirely to smelting works and fabrication yards, the horizon broken only by chimney stacks and the identical rooflines of worker housing blocks. Little distinguishes one district from the next, and the world's few visitors and its own citizens alike describe it, without much argument, as thoroughly dull. The industry here is old and steady rather than prosperous, turning out finished metal goods in volume but with none of the ceremony or spectacle found on richer worlds. Weather, geography and architecture all seem to have settled into the same flat sameness that gives the place its reputation.
152.inhabitants: The Bony Birds who crowd Isatre's factory towns are thin-framed and quick-moving, bred by generations of shift work into a population that values punctuality over conversation. The dictatorship keeps assignments fixed and movement between districts limited, so most live out their working lives within sight of the plant that employs them. Comfortable wages and steady rations have made them dependable rather than restless, content to let the world's dullness go unremarked.

153.description: Aona's small landmass is dominated by a chain of great volcanoes, their slopes terraced with distilleries that draw on mineral-rich runoff to produce the lethal brandy that carries the world's name across the trade lanes. Heavy industry clusters in the lowland basins between the peaks, where refineries and manufactories run alongside the vineyards and stillhouses. Settlement is dense and vertical, cities built up rather than out to spare the fertile volcanic soil for cultivation.
153.inhabitants: The population, large harmless felines, organizes itself through the loose consultative bodies typical of a confederacy, with guilds of distillers and industrialists holding considerable local sway. Wealth here runs deep and shows in the polish of the cities and the confidence of a people whose work has made their world's name synonymous with a particular, potent luxury.

154.description: Isinor's oceans have earned a reputation that travels far beyond the system, their waters carrying colors and currents unlike those found on any comparable world. The seas dominate a large world of modest means, leaving the scattered farming communities to work thin, salt-crusted coastal soil between fishing seasons. Settlements spread widely along the shorelines rather than clustering inland, following the fabled waters rather than the poor land behind them. Confederacy administrators oversee a population that remains agricultural in habit though the ocean, not the field, is what visitors ask after.
154.inhabitants: The frogs that share the shoreline are slow-moving and utterly harmless, tolerated as neighbors rather than pests by the human farmers and fishers. People here get by on modest means, their days shaped by tides and planting rather than industry, and the loose Confederacy rule leaves local custom, not distant law, to settle most matters.

155.description: Uszaa's industrial belts spread across a sizeable landmass in loose, unplanned clusters, the legacy of factories raised and abandoned as local fortunes shifted without any central authority to coordinate them. Refineries and smelters sit close to the forests that host the Uszaaian tree grub, a pale burrowing larva harvested from bark hives and prized locally as both food and curiosity. The world has no unifying government to speak of, so settlements negotiate their own terms with passing traders, and a peculiar, almost ceremonial hospitality toward outsiders has taken hold as one of the few things every faction agrees on.
155.inhabitants: Uszaaians work hard, unglamorous industrial jobs under no fixed authority, forming loose compacts and local militias to keep the factories running and the peace more or less intact. Despite the grinding routine of their economy, they are famous for turning almost giddy in the presence of visitors, plying them with tree grub delicacies and unsolicited tours of works and warrens alike.

156.description: Aanbiat is a large world given over almost entirely to agriculture, its lowlands quilted with the long-established rows of the Aanbiatian Mained banana plantations that have made the planet's name across the region. The soil is thin and the climate unkind in patches, so yields are modest and the plantations are worked with old, careful methods rather than heavy machinery. Settlements sit strung along the fertile belts in loose lines rather than dense clusters, following the plantations rather than any planned grid.
156.inhabitants: The population is large for a world this poor, and most households have some stake in the banana harvest, whether as growers, packers or haulers. Elected councils at the district level manage water rights and harvest schedules, and the colonials take a plain pride in the plantations' age, treating the crop as an inheritance to be maintained rather than a business to be grown.

157.description: Bemaera is a small world of thin farmland scattered between rock and scrub, worked in patches rather than in any organized expanse. Its holdings answer to no single authority, each hamlet and croft falling under its own petty arrangement, which suits a population too dispersed for anything grander. It is known chiefly for the Rebeoid, a native growth or creature of genuine lethality that the locals treat with a carelessness bordering on the absurd. Little else distinguishes the place beyond its poverty and its primitive tools, both plainly visible in how its settlements are built and maintained.
157.inhabitants: The lizards of Bemaera live in small, self-governing clusters with little contact beyond their own fields, and centuries of fragmented rule have left them indifferent to any wider order. They are widely regarded, even by their own neighbors, as an unusually silly people, prone to games and jokes in the presence of the very dangers that kill them. Poverty and primitive means have not made them grim; if anything, they meet both with a shrug and a laugh.

158.description: Inines is a large world given over almost entirely to industry, its landscape dominated by fabrication complexes and processing works that stretch across continents once occupied by open ground. Settlement follows a rigid administrative pattern, with dense housing blocks arranged around the factories they serve. Despite its advanced infrastructure and considerable wealth, the world has a reputation among traders and travellers as a tedious place, its output steady and its routines unchanging year after year.
158.inhabitants: The insect population labours under a collectivized industrial order, each hive-descended commune assigned its output quotas and its place in the production chain. Life follows the rhythm of the factories rather than any season or custom, and the wealth generated flows back into the system rather than into any visible leisure or spectacle. Conversation among the inhabitants tends toward production figures and schedules, a habit outsiders find as wearing as the world itself.

159.description: Edzaon's oceans and river systems carry a mineral toxicity that has earned the water its lethal reputation, forcing every settlement to be built around sealed reservoirs and imported or heavily filtered supply. The world's industry, mostly smelting and heavy fabrication, clusters near these guarded water sources rather than near ore fields, giving the settled regions a scattered, fortified look. Periodic solar activity disrupts power grids and communications across the sizeable landmass, and older facilities are built low and shielded against the worst of it.
159.inhabitants: Local lords hold the water rights and the foundries alike, binding laborers to particular works much as land was once bound to a manor, and advancement depends more on a lord's favor than on skill alone. Life is hard but steady, and the workers who tend the reservoirs and furnaces take a grim pride in surviving conditions that would kill a careless outsider.

160.description: Leritean is a small world of thin soils and scattered holdings, worked by hand under the eye of local lords rather than machines. The land yields little of ordinary value, but a handful of dishes made from its stranger native plants and grubs have earned the world a modest name off-world, spoken of in the same breath as its poverty. Villages are few and far between, each bound to a manor or keep that takes its tithe in grain, meat, or labor.
160.inhabitants: The colonials live under oath to local lords, their lives measured out in seasons of planting and levy.
