Cooking here is not luxury but necessity, turning what the ground grudgingly gives into something worth eating, and it is this skill, honed by want rather than plenty, that has made its way into the wider galaxy's talk.

161.description: Veale's landmass is given over almost entirely to close-canopied forest, broken only where corporate holdings have cut clean geometric plantations into the green. Beneath the trees run the plantation towns, laid out along irrigation channels and processing rail lines that feed the agricultural combines controlling most of the surface. The forests themselves are managed rather than wild, cropped in rotation for timber, fibre and the shade-grown produce that has made the world's holding companies rich.
161.inhabitants: The frogs of Veale live and work within a strict corporate hierarchy, most of them employed from birth by whichever combine holds title to their district of forest. Advanced technology and steady wealth have made daily life comfortable, but ownership of land, water and canopy rights remains entirely in company hands, and the population's ambitions run largely along the career ladders those companies provide.

162.description: Edle's industrial belts ring its temperate lowlands, feeding factories that keep working even as districts change hands in the recurring civil disturbances that mark its history. The world's kitchens are legendary for their devotion to the food blender, an appliance produced here in every conceivable variation and refined to an obsessive standard. Its cities are dense, walled in sections, and rebuilt often, bearing the scars of successive uprisings against whichever faction currently holds the capital.
162.inhabitants: The population lives well by most measures, provided with advanced goods and comfortable housing, yet under a dictatorship that shifts hands violently and without warning. Edle's colonials are practical and resilient, keeping their workshops running and their tables set with elaborate blended dishes regardless of who claims to govern them that season.

163.description: Anlama's continents are given over almost entirely to refineries, foundries and the grid of housing blocks that serve them, a pattern repeated with such regularity across its sizeable landmass that little else distinguishes one district from the next. Governance is split among competing local authorities, each administering its own strip of factories and each keeping to procedures that rarely vary from one administration to another. The world has a settled, comfortable prosperity and every mark of advanced technology, yet visitors and residents alike describe it as a tedious little planet, its wealth generated with mechanical regularity and little else to show for it.
163.inhabitants: The population is made up of harmless, bug-eyed avians who staff the refineries and civic offices with unhurried patience, having long since adapted to lives governed by shift schedules and jurisdictional paperwork rather than ambition. Under so many small governments layered atop one another, they have become expert compilers of forms and keepers of routine, mild-tempered and rarely given to complaint.

164.description: Ribilebi is a large world whose surface is given over almost entirely to ocean, its landmasses reduced to a scatter of continental shelves and volcanic chains. Industrial complexes cluster along the coastlines, drawing on deep-water processing and mineral dredging to keep the state's foundries running. Despite the scale of its shipyards and refineries, the planet's fame rests less on output than on the goat soup simmered in coastal communes, a dish tied so closely to local identity that recipes are guarded between districts. Settlement remains thin, with most habitation strung along the shore in state-planned towns built around the ports and processing plants.
164.inhabitants: Labor is organized through collective enterprises, with quotas set for the coastal foundries and the goat herds kept on the scattered islands that supply the soup trade. Life follows the rhythm of shift work and communal kitchens, and pride in the local cuisine runs alongside pride in the output of the yards. Wealth is shared modestly but steadily, and most families measure standing by their place within the collective rather than by private means.

165.description: Relaes is a large world given over almost entirely to standardized manufacture, its continents divided into production zones that repeat the same grey pattern of foundries, dormitory blocks and canals from one horizon to the next. The climate is temperate and unremarkable, kept that way by decades of engineered atmospheric management, and the state has long since optimized away anything resembling variation in the daily routine. It is, by every account, a tedious place: the work is steady, the output is consistent, and nothing much happens.
165.inhabitants: The frog population lives under a planned economy that assigns labor and housing with the same flat efficiency applied to its factories, and most residents have accepted the predictability of it as the price of comfort. Wealth here is real but evenly spread and rarely spent on anything that would break the monotony, and conversation tends toward production quotas rather than ambition.

166.description: Dizaoner's broad continents host industrial districts strung along magnetic-shadow valleys, where cliffs and ridges offer some shelter from the solar storms that scour the open plains. Power grids are duplicated and buried wherever possible, since flares strong enough to blind orbital instruments arrive with little warning and can strip exposed relay towers bare. The world's many separate administrations each hold their own fortified industrial zones, and travel between them is timed around forecasts of ionospheric disturbance rather than distance. Factories here run in shifts dictated less by demand than by whichever hours are judged safest to keep workers above ground.
166.inhabitants: The heavy-framed, fat-bodied population favours thick-walled housing and short commutes between shielded worksites, a habit born of generations spent watching the sky for the next storm. Each local government manages its own warning systems and relief funds, and the comfortable wealth spread through the industrial economy owes much to the redundancy built into every factory and home. People here speak of the sun the way other worlds speak of weather, with resigned familiarity rather than fear.

167.description: Razaar's fields spread across low, unbroken plains under a sky that rarely varies from a flat, colorless grey. Farmsteads sit far apart along dirt roads, each one raising the same grain and the same tired livestock as the last, and nothing about the routine has changed for as long as anyone can remember. Travelers who pass through find little to remark on beyond the sameness of it, which is precisely the reputation the world has earned itself. Its few towns are little more than grain depots with a name attached.
167.inhabitants: The colonials who work Razaar's land answer to a ruling authority that concerns itself chiefly with grain quotas and little else, leaving daily life to unfold without interference or improvement. Generations of primitive tools and thin returns have made them patient, unhurried people who expect nothing dramatic from a day and are rarely disappointed. They speak plainly, when they speak at all, and measure a good year simply by the absence of a bad one.

168.description: Enonla's compact landmass is carved into fortified sectors, each held by a rival division of the same parent corporation, and the fighting between them has gutted much of the world's industrial base. Refineries and foundries stand half-operational, their output diverted to the factions rather than to trade, which leaves the world's considerable wealth locked in vaults and shipping contracts rather than in working plant. Advanced fabrication lines still run in the sectors under firm control, producing goods of real sophistication even as neighbouring districts burn. Dense housing blocks, built to hold the world's crowded population, now double as barracks and checkpoints.
168.inhabitants: The bug-eyed lobsters of Enonla are a mild, unaggressive species, holding no grievance of their own in the war fought over their world by competing boards and shareholder militias. Under corporate charter law they are bound as labour to whichever division controls their district, and most simply keep to their assigned work, tending machinery that changes ownership with the front lines. Their patience under repeated occupation is remarked upon even by the officers who requisition their labour.

169.description: Isanlequ is a large world of thin farmsteads scattered across vast tracts of empty land, its holdings barely scratching the surface of the terrain available to them. The soil yields modest grain and root harvests, most of it consumed by the manors that claim it under the old feudal obligations. A wasting sickness moves through the villages in slow, recurring waves, leaving whole hamlets thinned or abandoned, and no lord has yet found a cure or even a name for it. What little wealth exists is spent on wards and remedies that do not work.
169.inhabitants: The furred, feline folk of Isanlequ live under a strict hierarchy of manor lords and bound tenants, with primitive tools and long custom governing nearly everything they do. The disease has made them wary of strangers and of each other, and many villages keep to themselves, burying their sick quietly and saying little about it.

170.description: Tibecea's industry is parceled out among hereditary holdings, each lord's works turning out machined goods under charters older than the current tenants. Smokestacks rise from walled manufactories set between terraced fields and grazing land, the two economies sharing the same average-sized world without much overlap. The Tibeceaian edible poet, a delicacy cultivated in the shadow of these works, has carried the world's name further than any of its exports of metal or cloth. Settlements remain moderate in size, clustered around the manors that still hold the deeds to the land beneath them.
170.inhabitants: Colonial families work the forges and the fields alike, bound to their lord's charter more by custom than by law, and take a plain pride in a livelihood that leaves little room for excess. Wages keep pace with need but rarely much beyond it, and the cultivation of the poet, tended with the same care as any craft passed down through a guild, is spoken of with more warmth than the factories that pay the bills.

171.description: Sotera's arable belts ring temperate lowlands given over almost entirely to collective grain and orchard estates, their harvests feeding both the population and the distilleries that produce the world's brandy. Settlement follows the old planning logic of the collectives: grid towns set at regular intervals along irrigation canals, each with its own granary, clinic and distillery hall. The brandy, cask-aged in state warehouses before release, carries a reputation for potency that the local co-operatives neither confirm nor deny.
171.inhabitants: Labor on Sotera is organized through agricultural collectives that assign fields, orchards and distillery shifts on rotating schedules, leaving little room for private enterprise but ensuring steady comfort for most households. The people are practical and unhurried, proud of their harvests and quietly amused by outsiders' reactions to the brandy's strength.

172.description: Esveor's continents sit scattered across broad pink oceans, the colour born of mineral salts and micro-organisms that stain the water from shore to horizon. Farmsteads and hamlets are spread thinly across the land, each answering to its own local authority rather than any single planetary rule. Beyond the coastal towns, the world is best known for the improvised zero-gravity hockey leagues that draw crowds from settlements otherwise isolated from one another by distance and custom.
172.inhabitants: The small, rounded, placid humanoids who work Esveor's fields and shallows favour cooperation over ambition, trading produce between rival districts with little regard for the patchwork of governments that claim them. Their primitive tools and modest means keep most households simply getting by, and their tempers, like their bodies, run soft and unhurried.

173.description: Esteonbi's industrial belts run beneath ridged domes and radiation-hardened towers, a defense against the solar flares that lash the upper atmosphere without warning. Power grids are triple-shielded and staggered across regions so that a flare taking down one district leaves the rest running. Its cities spread wide and low rather than tall, favouring buried transit and shielded courtyards over open plazas.
173.inhabitants: The small black slimy frogs native to the world are famously withdrawn, conducting civic business through written proxies and remote assemblies rather than face-to-face council. Their democracy functions largely through distributed, low-visibility committees, well suited to a population that prefers not to be seen conducting its affairs. Wealth here is channelled quietly into shielding and redundancy rather than display, in keeping with a people who avoid attention even in their prosperity.

174.description: Xeesenri is a small world of thin soils and scattered clearings, worked by hand and draft animal rather than machine. Its farms lie far apart, each holding walled off from its neighbours by hedgerow or fence, and no central authority marks roads, borders, or towns. What little is grown barely feeds the colony itself, and the surplus that does exist rarely leaves a farmer's own gate.
174.inhabitants: Without government or law beyond the household, the colonials of Xeesenri have settled into a wary, withdrawn manner, keeping to their own plots and avoiding strangers and each other alike. Visitors who linger near a farmstead report doors shut, voices lowered, and a general reluctance to be seen at all, a shyness so pronounced it has become the one thing outsiders remember about the place.

175.description: Oresle's continents are dominated by a chain of great volcanoes whose slopes feed the smelters and foundries clustered along the ash-rich lowlands. Industry here has never matched the wealth flowing through its ports, and much of the manufacturing base shows the wear of decades without proper reinvestment. A persistent and virulent disease has moved through the heavily populated lowland cities in repeated waves, straining the world's advanced medical infrastructure even as it fails to touch the isolated highland settlements. Quarantine walls and rebuilt districts stand as a permanent feature of the urban skyline.
175.inhabitants: The confederated council governments spend more on containment and relief than on the aging factories that employ most of the population, leaving a workforce skilled but under-resourced. Colonials here are known for a certain grim practicality, having lived for generations alongside both the volcanic hazard and the recurring outbreaks, and civic life still bears the discipline of quarantine-era rationing.

176.description: Ervein packs its industrial works and residential blocks onto a landmass barely large enough to hold them, so refineries stand shoulder to shoulder with tenement rows and rooftop markets. Effluent channels cut through every district, carrying the runoff of foundries and processing plants toward reclamation ponds that never quite keep pace with demand. The confederated councils that govern the world have grown rich on the output of these works, even as the world itself has become a byword for grime and stench among neighboring systems.
176.inhabitants: Erveiners work in shifts that never fully end, rotating through factories and reclamation crews under contracts negotiated by their district councils. Prosperity has made them proud rather than apologetic, and they speak of their world's foulness with the same blunt satisfaction they bring to its ledgers.

177.description: Larais holds vast tracts of grain and root farmland under a permanent haze of processing smoke, its soil rich but its cities notorious for accumulated refuse that the state has never bothered to clear. Settlements sprawl in dense, low tiers around the collection depots, with open channels of waste running between them that the developed sanitation systems were meant to handle and no longer do. The world exports steadily and eats well by its own measure, even as its ports and markets remain some of the foulest-smelling in the region.
177.inhabitants: The rodent population works the fields and depots under a dictatorship that rewards output and ignores upkeep, so households live in real comfort while the streets around them decay. Generations of this arrangement have bred a population that is diligent, orderly, and largely indifferent to filth it no longer notices.

178.description: Anxebiza spreads its farmland across a sizeable landmass, an unremarkable dump whose reputation rests on tired soil, dull weather and the flat sameness of its grain belts rather than anything that draws notice. Corporate holdings quarter the plains into estates, each stamped with a company crest and worked to modest, functional methods rather than any finer craft. The towns that serve these estates are plain and repetitive, built to house labor and store yield rather than to be looked at.
178.inhabitants: The furry rodent population lives well enough by the standards of their contracts, comfortable but tied closely to the corporate estates that employ them from birth. Life follows the harvest calendar and the company ledger in equal measure, and pride in the work has long since worn down to simple routine.

179.description: Diedar spreads across wide plains and river basins given over to grain and livestock, its farms worked without the aid of heavy machinery. Villages and market towns sit apart from one another, connected by dirt roads that column of refugees and militia alike have worn deeper than any cart. Fields near the old provincial borders lie burned or abandoned, and granaries that once fed the whole world now serve only whichever faction holds them this season.
179.inhabitants: The colonials maintain their elected councils in the towns still standing, though loyalty to any single government has fractured along old regional lines. Farmers keep working the land between skirmishes, wary and quick to abandon a field at the sound of gunfire, and most families count someone lost or missing to the fighting.

180.description: Eninre's cramped landmasses hold factory towns that once fed a wider trade network but now run at a fraction of their old output, their furnaces kept alight by whichever faction controls the ore lines that week. Settlements are dense and walled, built close around the smelters and refineries that remain the only reliable source of work, with the spaces between them given over to burned fields and checkpoints that change hands often. The civil war that defines the world has no capital and no front line, only a shifting patchwork of holdings fought over street by street and factory by factory.
180.inhabitants: Without any central authority to answer to, the population survives through local militias, factory bosses and neighbourhood councils that trade loyalty for protection and rations. Skilled labour is common thanks to the world's developed industry, but little of that skill translates into comfort, and most colonials measure success simply in staying fed, housed and out of the fighting.

181.description: Bibe is a middling world of scattered farmsteads and fallow ground, its fields kept more by habit than by any coordinating authority. What order exists is local and temporary, worked out village by village with no government above it. The place is known across the trade lanes for a brandy distilled fierce enough to kill the careless drinker, and less happily for a sickness that moves through its settlements without pattern or cure.
181.inhabitants: Colonials here farm and distill in equal measure, keeping to small kin-groups since no wider law binds them together. Poverty and primitive means leave little margin against the disease that recurs through their settlements, and the brandy they are famous for is brewed as much out of grim necessity as tradition.

182.description: Diquxe presents a landscape dominated by ancient mountain ranges, worn to jagged, weathered peaks by ages of erosion, yet the world remains geologically restless. Frequent earthquakes shake the industrial belts strung along the valley floors, cracking foundations and forcing constant rebuilding. Its factories and refineries operate behind reinforced walls and quake-braced towers, a grim accommodation to ground that never quite settles. Wealth from heavy manufacturing has built dense, orderly cities that spread across the lowlands between the peaks.
182.inhabitants: The horned lobsters of Diquxe govern themselves through elected councils that debate building codes and disaster funding as often as trade policy, a reflection of lives spent rebuilding what the tremors take. Long exposure to instability has bred a calm, practical temperament, more concerned with structural reinforcement than with spectacle. Industrial labor and civic administration occupy most of the population, and pride in engineering solutions runs deep among them.

183.description: Sorace carries the weight of a corporate charter that never quite reconciled its factions, and the resulting war has scarred the industrial districts that ring its cities. Refineries and assembly yards operate behind barricades, their output diverted as often to militia as to market, while advanced fabrication plants sit half-idle for want of secure supply lines. The wealth generated by controlling shareholders sits uneasily alongside crumbling worker housing, a contradiction the fighting has only sharpened.
183.inhabitants: The Fierce Slimy Lobsters that crowd Sorace's hab-tiers are shaped by generations under competing boardroom banners, quick to defend territory and quicker to distrust rival directorates. Labor here is disciplined and technically skilled, but loyalty runs to faction before firm, and firm before world, a habit the corporate charter has never managed to break.

184.description: Rain forest covers most of Anxeonis, broken only by cleared basins where the agricultural estates cut their fields from the canopy. The soil beneath the trees is rich enough to feed the estates without much fertilizer, and the climate holds warm and wet through most of the year with little variation. Settlements sit along the cleared river edges, small and spread thin against the scale of the forest around them, connected by roads that flood in the heavier seasons.
184.inhabitants: The Black Fat Insects that work the estates labor under a single ruling authority that sets quotas for the forest clearances and the harvests alike, and little of the wealth those harvests generate seems to reach the settlements themselves. Life here is organized around the growing season and the directives that come down from the capital, with modest tools and modest comforts to show for the effort.

185.description: Riantiat spreads wide beneath thin agricultural cover, its farmland broken by scrub and rangeland where the spotted wolf still hunts unchecked. The edible grub is cultivated and gathered across the lowlands, a staple crop that has never developed beyond subsistence scale. Villages and market towns sit far apart across the great size of the world, linked by dirt roads and river crossings rather than any central authority. Tools and techniques remain primitive, and the land is worked much as it has been for generations.
185.inhabitants: The Horned Birds live under a loose confederacy of local councils, with no strong central government to direct or tax the scattered farming communities. Poverty is common and expected, and most households divide their labor between grub cultivation and warding off the spotted wolf from herds and stores. Self-reliance and suspicion of outside authority mark the temperament of the farming clans, who settle most disputes among themselves.

186.description: Zarece turns slowly under a flat, unremarkable sky, its cleared fields and scattered pastures spread across low hills that repeat for great distances without variation. Farming is done here largely as it has always been done, with hand tools and draft animals working plots that yield modest grain and root crops. The scattered farmsteads and market towns that make up its settlements are functional and identical to a fault, and little of note has ever happened here to change that.
186.inhabitants: The population, fierce black felines organized loosely under a confederacy of local councils, spend their days on the unglamorous work of subsistence farming and small trade between neighboring holdings. Poverty and primitive tools leave little room for ambition beyond the next harvest, and the councils exist mainly to settle boundary disputes and divide what little surplus there is. Even their tempers, sharp as they are, rarely find cause to flare in a place where so little changes from one season to the next.

187.description: Maesin spreads across a wide expanse of scrubland and cracked flats, its holdings thin and far apart under a sky the color of old paper. What farming exists clings to shallow river cuts and depends on rains that arrive late as often as not. No authority governs the place beyond whatever arrangement neighbors strike among themselves, and little effort has gone into making it more than it is. Traders who file reports on Maesin tend to use the same word twice: unremarkable.
187.inhabitants: The world's small furry rodent population lives in loose burrow-colonies scattered near the water cuts, foraging the scrub and storing what little the soil yields against the dry months. With no government to organize labor or defend a claim, each colony manages its own patch of ground and mostly leaves its neighbors alone.

188.description: Rain forest covers most of the land surface of Tibionis, broken only where clearings have been cut for farmsteads and market towns. The canopy sustains a agricultural economy built around herding, though the Tibionisian deadly goat, bred and grazed in fenced enclosures cut from the forest edge, gives the world its name in trade circles far beyond its own skies. Settlements follow river valleys and forest roads rather than any planned grid, giving the populated regions a scattered, organic look from above.
188.inhabitants: The people, furry rodents by descent, govern themselves through elected assemblies that argue endlessly over forest clearance rights and grazing quotas. Comfortable rather than rich, they take evident pride in husbandry skill, and goat handlers who work the deadly breed without injury are locally regarded with a respect usually reserved for pilots or engineers.

189.description: Gelegeus is a small, thin-soiled world where scattered holdings work terraces and dry valleys against a climate that gives little back. Its farms cluster loosely around a handful of stills where the local enorinbi fruit is fermented into brandy, the one product that carries the world's name beyond its own sky. There is no central authority; the settlements answer to their own councils and headmen, and roads between them are little more than cart tracks.
189.inhabitants: The colonials are farmers first, distillers second, and their loyalties run no further than the valley or terrace they were born to. Primitive tools and poor soil make for hard, unhurried lives, and what pride the world affords its people is bound up in the brandy each community claims to make better than its neighbors.

190.description: Diora spreads across a wide radius of factory belts and dormitory towns, its horizon flattened by refinery stacks rather than any notable geography. State planning has organized production into regional collectives, each turning out machined goods without any particular specialty or flourish. Nothing in its climate, terrain or output distinguishes it from a hundred other industrial worlds under similar management; the planners themselves describe it as adequate and leave it at that.
190.inhabitants: The population works fixed shifts in collectively run plants, housed in uniform blocks assigned by the regional bureau rather than chosen. Modest technology and comfortable but unremarkable wealth have produced a steady, unambitious workforce, more concerned with meeting quotas than with distinction.

191.description: Rigeti's broad plains and marshlands yield only meager grain and root crops, hampered by poor soil and erratic rains under feudal lords who claim the surplus. Villages cluster around fortified manor holds, their middens and open drainage ditches left to fester in the damp heat. The world has earned its low reputation honestly: refuse accumulates at the edge of every hamlet and the lowland air carries a settled taint of rot. Isolated homesteads dot the vast, largely empty interior, linked by little more than mud tracks.
191.inhabitants: The peasantry owes labor and tithe to local lords who hold sole claim to what little machinery exists, so fieldwork is done mostly by hand and beast. Generations of subsistence farming under feudal obligation have bred a stoic, insular population with little expectation of comfort. Few venture beyond their own holding, and fewer still imagine that life elsewhere is any better.

192.description: Begeabi is a small, dry world of cracked plains and shallow river valleys, its soil thin and reluctant to yield much beyond hardy grain and root crops. Settlements are few and far between, each clustered around a fortified keep that holds the surrounding fields under a local lord's claim. Poverty is the common condition here, and little beyond subsistence farming and small tithes of produce moves between the scattered holdings.
192.inhabitants: The lizard population lives under a patchwork of feudal lords whose authority rests more on ceremony and old grudge than on any real force, and much of daily life is given over to elaborate, pointless ritual that outsiders would call nonsense but the lizards treat with total seriousness. Farming and fealty structure their days, but games, riddles and absurd formal disputes fill the rest, passed down through generations as though they were law.

193.description: Orrere is a sizeable world of thin, exhausted soils and long dry seasons, given over to grain and tuber plots that yield little beyond subsistence. What surplus exists is fermented into the Orrerian vicious brew, a harsh spirit distilled in cooperative sheds across the lowland districts and shipped out under the corporate label that owns most of the arable land. Settlements are strung along irrigation channels in dense, low rows of housing, built cheaply and added to as the population has grown past what the land can properly feed.
193.inhabitants: Most people work land or stills leased from the governing corporation, paid in scrip and produce rather than wealth of any real kind. Life is plain and closely managed, and the brewing of the vicious spirit is treated less as tradition than as one more quota to be met each season.

194.description: Beti is a small world dominated by a scattering of active and dormant volcanic cones, their vents releasing gases in patterns that shift unpredictably from season to season. Between the lava fields and ash slopes, farmers work terraced plots of mineral-rich soil, coaxing a modest but steady harvest from ground still warm underfoot. The planet's mountain lobstoid, a hardy crustacean adapted to the heated streams and sulfurous pools, has become the subject of considerable scientific and culinary curiosity offworld. Settlements cluster along the cooler valley floors, well back from the more temperamental peaks.
194.inhabitants: Life under the dictatorship is orderly but constrained, with land allotments and lobstoid harvesting rights controlled by local administrators loyal to the ruling authority. Most colonials are farmers or trappers, weathered by proximity to the volcanic terrain and accustomed to sudden changes in ground temperature and air quality. They speak of the mountains with a mix of resentment and pride, aware that the same forces that threaten their fields also draw curiosity and modest income from beyond the world.

195.description: Gerete's cramped landmass forced its industry upward and inward long ago, and the small world now carries dense manufacturing districts stacked beneath domed skylines. Its position leaves it exposed to unpredictable solar activity, which periodically disrupts orbital traffic and surface power grids alike, a hazard the planners never fully engineered around. Despite this, or perhaps because of it, Gerete is fabled across the region for its Zero-G cricket leagues, played in shielded stadiums built to withstand the same flares that plague the rest of the world. No single authority governs the whole surface; instead overlapping jurisdictions parcel out the industrial zones and orbital works among themselves.
195.inhabitants: The population lives well by regional standards, its wealth built on layered industry and the constant negotiation between competing local governments. Gerete's people are practical about the solar hazard, treating flare warnings as routine business rather than emergency, and reserve their real passion for the cricket leagues that give the world its fame beyond its own skies.

196.description: Qucerere is a sizeable world given over almost entirely to grain and root crops, its landmass divided into collective holdings that stretch to the horizon in even, regulated strips. Settlements sit at fixed intervals along the main irrigation lines, each built to the same state plan and each much like the last. Little distinguishes one district from another beyond the crop rotation posted on the local board, and the planet's reputation as a tedious place is earned honestly, day after identical day.
196.inhabitants: The population works assigned plots under quota, comfortable enough in food and housing but with few surprises in either. Colonial by origin and communal by law, they take a certain grim pride in output figures and little else, and conversation tends toward the weather, the harvest, and not much more.

197.description: Xeoner is a small agricultural world of collective farms and grain stores set beneath grey, unremarkable skies. The land is given over almost entirely to cultivation, its low hills terraced and its plains divided into uniform plots that yield a steady but unspectacular harvest. Settlements are laid out in the same blocky, functional pattern from one district to the next, a repetition that has made the world proverbial for its sameness. Nothing about Xeoner invites a second look, and its own inhabitants would be the first to admit it.
197.inhabitants: The people work the fields and grain depots under collective assignment, their days ordered by quota rather than season. Getting by is the general condition, and most seem resigned to it, taking a certain flat pride in doing steady, unglamorous work without complaint.

198.description: Xezaor packs refineries, fabrication yards and casino towers into a landmass barely large enough to hold them, so that smoke from one district drifts directly into the neon of the next. Its fame rests on the casino strips that ring the equatorial cities, walled compounds of tiered gaming floors run under charters that change hands with each shift in local rule. Beneath the glare, the industrial works that actually pay for the lighting run day and night, their output shipped out through crowded ports wedged between the gambling districts. The world is carved into overlapping jurisdictions, each with its own tariffs, courts and casino licenses, so that a street can change law twice in a short walk.
198.inhabitants: The large horned birds that crowd Xezaor's cities move between shift work in the foundries and long hours dealing cards or tending the gaming floors, and most hold some stake in both economies. Comfortable wealth and constant competition among the local governments have made them shrewd about contracts and unbothered by the sight of fortunes won or lost nearby. They speak of their home city's charter the way others speak of nationality, and guard it accordingly.

199.description: Ritila's casino districts spread across the equatorial belt, their neon-strip facades and pressurised gaming halls run in parallel with the world's foundries and refineries. The same crowded transit tunnels that carry shift workers between factory and gaming floor also carry the wasting sickness that has settled into the population and refuses to lift, despite the dictatorship's periodic quarantines and purges of suspected carriers. Away from the casino strips, the industrial districts run grey and functional, their smokestacks visible even through the haze that hangs over the gaming quarter's lights.
199.inhabitants: Most residents work double lives, tending assembly lines by day and dealing cards or minding tables by night, their earnings watched closely by a state that taxes both wages and winnings. A visible portion of the populace bears the marks of the lingering illness, kept from the wealthier casino patrons by screened corridors and separate entrances, and there is a quiet, practiced resignation in how people speak of it, as something to be managed rather than cured.

200.description: Edorte spreads its farmland across a sizeable landmass under skies dulled by irrigation haze and processing exhaust, and for all its harvests it remains, by common reckoning, an unremarkable dump. The land is given over almost entirely to corporate estates, vast grids of grain and fibre crop run by agricultural holding companies whose logos mark every silo and water tower. Towns exist mainly as service points for the estates, functional and repetitive, built to a standard plan and showing little variation from one to the next.
200.inhabitants: The Harmless Felines who work Edorte's fields and processing lines do so under contracts issued by the same handful of holding companies that own the land itself, their lives organized around planting and harvest schedules rather than any civic calendar. Comfortable wages and steady advanced-tech conveniences temper the monotony, producing a population that is well-fed, orderly, and largely indifferent to the world's dull reputation beyond its borders.'}

201.description: Zaalela is a world of open range and scattered holdings, its farmland divided among manors that owe allegiance to local lords. Herds of goats move across the dry pasture under the watch of herders on foot, and the animals form the backbone of both diet and trade within the world's own borders. The soup made from them, thickened with local roots and spiced with wild herbs, is spoken of with more pride than anything else the world produces. Settlements are small and far apart, built around wells and threshing yards rather than any central town.
201.inhabitants: The Fierce Harmless Horned Lizards who hold Zaalela live under a strict hierarchy of landed lords and bound tenants, their labor spent almost entirely on herding, planting and the slow work of the soil. Fierce in temperament but without malice, they settle disputes through ritual displays rather than violence, and reserve their warmth for kin, herd and the shared pot of soup simmering over a communal fire.

202.description: Biisorte's factories cluster along river deltas where the fabled Biisortian lethal water is drawn, distilled, and shipped out under heavy seal despite the toxicity that gives it its name. The same water table has bred a persistent contagion that moves through the lowland works and has never been fully checked, so entire districts stand fenced and unentered. Refineries and smelters dominate the skyline of the larger towns, their smoke mixing with quarantine flags strung along the approach roads. Modest tooling and feudal land grants keep production steady but never expanding, since no lord risks his holding to push further into the tainted ground.
202.inhabitants: Labour here is bound to hereditary estates, with workers owing service to the lord who holds the refinery lease and little say in where they are posted. Generations spent near the poisoned water have made the colonials fatalistic about illness, treating quarantine and loss as ordinary costs of the trade rather than crises. Wealth is thin and shared unevenly, and most measure a good year by how few names are added to the sick-lists.

203.description: Beesor's crust is unstable across most of its small landmass, and tremors severe enough to level unreinforced structures strike with grim regularity. The state has answered this by building low, heavily braced factory blocks and habitation blocks, all raised on shock-dampened foundations, ringing the industrial districts that keep the world's furnaces and assembly lines running. Its wealth comes from disciplined output rather than any accident of geography, extracted from workers and machinery alike despite the ground beneath them refusing to stay still.
203.inhabitants: The population lives under a planning bureau that treats quake preparedness as a form of civic duty, with labor brigades trained equally for the assembly floor and for emergency shoring work. Long exposure to sudden loss has bred a population that is stoic about property and fiercely attached to the collective, since rebuilding after a bad tremor is understood as everyone's task, not the state's alone.

204.description: Oresqu is a sizeable industrial world of mixed factory belts and residential blocks, its skyline broken by the offices of the many jurisdictions that share administration of the surface. No single authority governs the whole; instead a patchwork of local governments trade regulations and tariffs across shifting borders that rarely disrupt the steady output of goods. The world is mildly noted beyond its own system for the elaborate courtship customs observed among its population, rituals that draw academic curiosity more than tourism.
204.inhabitants: The rodents of Oresqu are industrious and clannish, organizing themselves into extended family enterprises that double as the basic unit of local politics. Comfortable wealth and advanced technology have given them time to formalize their mating traditions into structured, almost ceremonial affairs, distinct from one district to the next depending on which government holds sway there.

205.description: Xeququti's crust is riven by fault lines that shrug and rattle in constant, unpredictable spasms, so that its factories and tenements are built low, braced, and rebuilt often. The industrial base, cramped onto a small landmass, produces goods of little refinement despite the advanced tools behind them, the plants themselves half in ruin from the last serious tremor. Settlements cluster tightly around the more stable bedrock, forming dense, layered districts that seem to lean on one another for support.
205.inhabitants: The large frogs of Xeququti govern themselves through crowded assemblies where every district sends its voice, a habit of consultation born of having to rebuild together after each disaster. Wealth here sits oddly alongside worn machinery and cracked foundations, and the population has grown practical and unsentimental about property, since any structure may be rubble within a season.

206.description: Maises is a sizeable world of aging refineries and cracked processing yards, its industry outlasting the authority that once ran it. The famed Maisesian lethal water is distilled here in small, guarded batches, prized off-world even as the settlements around its extraction sites struggle under a disease with no cure and no quarantine to slow it. Without a government to coordinate relief or repair, plants run when their crews decide to run them, and whole districts sit dark and untended between one shift and the next. Housing sprawls close to the old factory belts, a legacy of a denser, better-ordered past the colony no longer has the means to maintain.
206.inhabitants: The population gets by through barter, favor, and improvised arrangements between rival work-crews who have effectively replaced the vanished administration. Sickness has hardened them to loss without dulling their pride in the toxic vintage that still carries the world's name outward, and most treat both the water and the disease as simply the price of living there.

207.description: Bierle's continents are given over almost entirely to refineries, foundries and the dense residential blocks that serve them, with little land left to wilderness save the fenced exclusion zones where the Edoid still breeds. The creature, venomous and disinclined to avoid populated areas, is treated as a standing hazard of daily life rather than a curiosity, and its image turns up on warning signs across every district. Wealth generated by the planet's manufacturing sector has built orderly, well-serviced cities, though much of the profit visibly returns into further plant construction rather than public leisure.
207.inhabitants: Confederacy administration keeps labour, safety codes and production quotas tightly coordinated across the industrial zones, and the workforce is generally well paid and well housed as a result. Off the factory floor, however, Bierlians are famous throughout neighbouring space for an irreverence that borders on the absurd, treating serious occasions with jokes and formal ones with pranks, as if the discipline demanded of them by day must be spent somewhere by night.

208.description: Arzaso presents little to distinguish it from a hundred other confederated industrial worlds: temperate belts given over to standardized factory towns, moderate seas, and a road and rail grid laid out with bureaucratic efficiency rather than any local character. Its manufacturing output is steady and diversified, feeding regional demand without dominating it. The planet's cities sprawl outward from administrative centers in near-identical concentric plans, a pattern repeated across its inhabited zones.
208.inhabitants: The population lives comfortably under confederate rule, well-off and well-supplied, with the settled ease of people whose world requires little defending or explaining. Generations of stable governance and steady industry have produced a citizenry more concerned with efficient administration than ambition, content to keep the factories running and the councils in session.

209.description: Teen is a small, dry world of scattered farmsteads and thin, terraced fields, worked by hand under a primitive order that has never mastered irrigation on any scale. Its settlements sit apart from one another across cracked lowlands, and the roads between them are unsafe and often unused, cut off by the civil war that has burned through the countryside for as long as anyone can recall. What little the soil yields is fought over as much as it is farmed, and whole districts have been left to the horned lizards that bask undisturbed on the ruined field walls.
209.inhabitants: The dictatorship holds its capital and little else, and its writ frays quickly beyond sight of the garrison towns, leaving most families to fend for themselves between raids. People here work the land in short, wary bursts, keep grain hidden rather than stored, and measure any stranger first by which faction they might belong to. Poverty and primitive tools make the harvest hard even without the fighting, and the fighting rarely stops.

210.description: Riredi's continents are given over almost entirely to smelting works, refineries, and the terraced slag-heaps that mark generations of extraction. Beneath the industrial haze the high ranges remain wild, and it is there that the Riredian mountain slug is farmed and hunted, prized off-world as a delicacy and studied for the mucus trade that has become the planet's other great export. The corporate charter that governs the world extracts most of what the factories produce, leaving the vast population dense in habitation but thin in personal means despite the fortunes recorded on the company ledgers.
210.inhabitants: The native furry insects that crowd Riredi's hab-blocks and slug-terraces work in shifts dictated by corporate schedule, tending both foundries and mountain slug pens with the same patient diligence. Harmless by temperament and long accustomed to distant ownership, they take evident pride in the slug harvest, the one product of their labor that carries the world's name with any fondness beyond its borders.

211.description: Teorge spreads its farmland across a large landmass under a flat, unremarkable sky, with little to break the monotony of furrowed fields and irrigation channels. Settlements sit at wide intervals, connected by dirt roads that see the same slow traffic of grain carts every season. The planet has earned a reputation, fairly or not, as a tedious little world, and nothing in its low hills or grey weather does much to argue against it. Farming towns repeat the same layout of granary, meeting hall, and market square with little variation from one district to the next.
211.inhabitants: The native Black Bony Lobsters work the fields and cooperatives with the patient, unhurried temperament of a people who vote on everything and rush at nothing. Living modestly and getting by rather than prospering, they take a quiet, stubborn pride in a world that offers little to boast about and ask for little more than its steady, predictable yield.

212.description: Vebege turns beneath a sun given to violent flares, and its scattered settlements are built low and shielded, cut into slopes and canyon walls where rock offers some cover from the surges. Its industry is modest and improvised, workshops and smelters strung between habitats rather than gathered into any real district, kept running by whatever machinery has survived import and repair. The mountain ranges that shelter its settlements are also home to the Vebegian mountain lobstoid, a hardy creature mildly fabled beyond the system despite the world's general poverty and isolation.
212.inhabitants: With no central authority to organize relief or defense, the colonials of Vebege rely on kin and neighboring holds when the solar weather turns bad, and grudges over shared shielding or scavenged parts run long. Work is hard and often dangerous, and most people measure a household's standing by how well its walls have held rather than by any coin it keeps.

213.description: Worn ranges of ancient rock cross the small world of Xeenle, their slopes stripped and scarred by furnaces and smelters that answer to no central authority. The industry here is crude and improvised, workshops bolted together from salvage rather than built to plan, scattered thin across the foothills where the ground is stable enough to hold them. A wasting sickness moves through the population in slow waves, and no settlement has found a way to stop it or even fully explain it.
213.inhabitants: The large frogs of Xeenle organize themselves into loose work-bands rather than towns, trading labor and ore between furnace sites with no ruling council to arbitrate disputes. Life expectancy is shortened by the disease that moves among them, and most measure wealth in tools and fuel rather than coin, since there is little coin to be had. Suspicion of outsiders and of each other runs deep, a habit born of scarcity and the absence of any law but local strength.

214.description: Arxeza's crust is restless, riven by fault lines that shudder through its industrial belts with little warning. Its cities are built low and reinforced, spread across wide plains rather than raised into towers, a concession learned through generations of collapsed districts. Factories and refineries here are designed to shut down and brace within moments, an engineering discipline that has become the world's quiet specialty. Even its wealth is measured partly in what has been rebuilt rather than simply accumulated.
214.inhabitants: Arxezan colonials live with a practical wariness bred of shifting ground, favouring sturdy construction and civic preparedness over ornament. The democracy governing them channels considerable industrial wealth into monitoring networks and rebuilding funds, and its citizens vote on such matters with unusual seriousness. Advanced technology and a dense, orderly population give the world an air of disciplined resilience rather than complacency.imeout

215.description: Edreor's land is given over almost entirely to cultivation, its plains divided into holdings that stretch toward a flat horizon under corporate survey markers. The Ra plant plantations are the oldest working land on the world, their rootstock said to predate the first corporate charters, and they remain the backbone of an economy built on export crops. Processing towns cluster around the pressing houses where Xexe fruit is rendered into the juice that has made the world's name, their layouts dictated by the old transport lines rather than any civic plan.
215.inhabitants: Most people work under contract to one agricultural concern or another, their lives structured by planting and pressing seasons rather than any calendar of their own choosing. The corporate state administers law, wages and housing alike, and the population has grown wealthy on the strength of it, though ownership of the land itself remains firmly with the companies rather than those who work it.

216.description: Esgerean's industrial belts and shielded settlements sit beneath skies that turn hostile without warning, as the system's star throws off flares capable of scrambling unshielded electronics and blacking out surface communications for hours at a time. Factories and habitation blocks alike are built low and armored, with hardened conduits running between them rather than open power lines. The disruptions have shaped the world's architecture more than its geography ever did, and entire districts are laid out around bunkered relay stations rather than around any natural feature.
216.inhabitants: Life under the dictatorship runs on schedules dictated as much by solar forecasts as by any decree, and the population has grown practiced at shutting down sensitive works at the first alert. Industrial routine and state control together produce a populace that is orderly, watchful, and comfortable enough materially to tolerate the arrangement without complaint.

217.description: Ditiza spreads across wide fertile plains and river basins given over almost entirely to cultivation, its farmland broken by the occasional processing town and grain depot. The world is reasonably fabled for a fermented concoction known locally as evil juice, brewed in vats behind half the farmhouses on the continent and shipped out in barrels stamped with cheerful, garish labels. Settlements are laid out in loose grids around communal silos and market squares, built more for function than for show, with little sign of the strain a large population might otherwise put on the land.
217.inhabitants: The Confederacy's loose hold over so many farming communities has bred a population accustomed to arguing at length before agreeing on anything, and comfortable wealth spread evenly enough that few see reason to hurry. Their ingrained silliness shows less in foolishness than in a fondness for elaborate jokes, harvest pageants, and drinking songs about the very juice that keeps their economy solvent.

218.description: Vast tropical forests girdle Anle's equator, their canopies broken by refinery towers and the smoke-stained sprawl of processing works that feed the confederacy's markets. Distilleries hidden beneath the forest canopy produce the Anlian evil brandy for which the world is infamous, a liquor fermented from forest sap and industrial byproduct alike. Away from the green belts, the land gives way to dense manufacturing districts stacked tight against one another, the inevitable result of a large world pressed to hold so many souls and so much machinery.
218.inhabitants: The Black Fat Insects who fill Anle's factories and forest plantations work under a confederate system that rewards output and cooperation over individual ambition, producing a population that is orderly, collective-minded, and comfortable with its wealth. Generations of industrial labour have left them practical and unsentimental, though the local brandy is spoken of with something close to reverence.

219.description: Onisqu is a large world of modest industry scattered thin across its surface, its factories run without central authority and without much ambition beyond keeping themselves fed with ore and fuel. The land is unremarkable, the sky unremarkable, and nothing in its geography or weather gives visitors reason to linger longer than trade requires. Settlements are few and widely spaced, each one a self-contained works surrounded by empty ground, and none of them has produced anything the rest of the galaxy finds worth remembering.
219.inhabitants: The Black Fat Insects that work these factories answer to no government beyond whatever arrangement keeps a given plant running, and poverty has made them practical rather than proud. They labour without complaint and without flourish, and the dullness of the place seems to suit a people who value a machine that works over a story worth telling.

220.description: Volcanic ranges run along much of the northern continent, their ash fields feeding soil that the world's founders once meant to farm rather than mine. The industrial base that grew up in their shadow has long since fallen behind more efficient worlds, leaving smokestack districts and refineries operating well under their old capacity. Beyond the cities, the shrews are the more immediate trouble: swarming, aggressive, and blamed for stripping fields and burrowing through the foundations of outlying settlements. Municipal authorities have given up eradication in favour of containment, and much of the land beyond the volcano belt is fenced against them.
220.inhabitants: The population, wealthy despite the faltering industry that once justified the colony, sustains itself through diversified holdings and off-world investment rather than the factories themselves. Elected councils argue publicly and often over shrew control budgets, a subject that dominates local politics more than any industrial policy. Long exposure to the vermin and the volcanoes has bred a population that is practical, wary of complacency, and unsentimental about the land it lives on.

221.description: Zasoceat's factories run under a patchwork of competing jurisdictions, each administration claiming a district and none claiming the waste that drifts between them. The result is an average-sized world thick with smoke, slag heaps, and canals of industrial runoff that no single authority will pay to clear. Its refineries and foundries turn a steady profit, but the money goes into shipping berths and boardrooms rather than the streets beneath them. The world's reputation for filth is not an exaggeration so much as an understatement worn smooth by repetition.
221.inhabitants: The population lives well by any material measure, drawing comfortable wages from the industrial output, but housing blocks sit hard against tailings ponds and open sewage channels that no jurisdiction wants to own. Colonials here have grown practical and thick-skinned about their surroundings, treating the grime as simply the cost of the work that pays them. Loyalties run to employer and district rather than to any planetary government, since none of the several administrations has ever managed to act as one.

222.description: Rilace spreads across gentle plains and low hills under a climate given to long, unchanging seasons, and little about its geography rewards a second look. Collective farms cover most of the arable land in grids that repeat from one horizon to the next, given over to grain and root crops rather than anything more colorful. The world's flatness and its steady, repetitive produce have earned it a reputation as a dull place, and little in its towns or its weather does anything to argue the point.
222.inhabitants: The colonials who work the collectives live under state quotas that reward steady output over ambition, and their days follow the same rotation of planting, harvest and inventory that their parents kept. Wealth here is modest and shared thinly, and the people are known less for complaint than for a flat, practical patience with the sameness of it all.

223.description: Beenri is a small, thinly peopled world whose farmland struggles against thin soil and neglect. The mountain Laxeedanoid dominates the horizon of its central plain, a peak of some local renown that draws pilgrims between fighting seasons. Beyond that modest fame, the world is chiefly known for the civil wars that pass through its scattered holdings like weather, burning fields as often as they are sown. Villages huddle low and close to their lords' halls, rebuilt again and again on the same ash.
223.inhabitants: The native population, soft-bodied and harmless insectile creatures, till their small plots under the rule of feuding lords who claim descent from older, grander houses now mostly forgotten. Loyalty here shifts with the season's fighting, and most families keep half an eye on the road and half on the crop, ready to abandon either at short notice.

224.description: Laeden's holdings are worked estates strung along river valleys, each bound to a manor lord who claims the harvest and the labour that produces it. Fields of grain and root crops dominate the lowlands, tended by hand and draft animal under a feudal order that has changed little in generations. The world's oddest export is cultural rather than material: recordings of its home-grown sit coms circulate well beyond its own sky, broadcast from manor halls with more ambition than budget.
224.inhabitants: Colonists here live under the authority of hereditary lords, farming rents owed in kind rather than coin, and the poverty of the arrangement shows in patched tools and mended roofs. Yet nearly every household keeps a food blender, however battered, treasured out of proportion to its use and passed down like a family heirloom. Evenings are given over to the manor's broadcast sit coms, which the tenantry follows with a devotion the fields rarely inspire.

225.description: Mariar's continents lie under a belt of tropical forest unlike any grown elsewhere, canopy strains engineered generations ago that outgrew their original purpose and now dominate the lowlands entirely. Beneath and around the forest, refineries and processing yards sprawl in irregular clearings, their output modest against the scale of the workforce housing that surrounds them. The corporation that administers the world has never managed to convert the forest's fame into matching industrial fortune, leaving the two faces of Mariar, verdant and grey, sitting uneasily side by side.
225.inhabitants: Dense city-blocks press close against the treeline, home to workers bound by contract to the company that owns most of the land beneath them. Wealth concentrates in administrative towers rather than in wages, and most residents speak of the forests less with wonder than with the resignation of people who live in its shadow rather than its glow.

226.description: Riiser is a large world whose industrial belts, built to feed a single centralized economy, now sit divided between factions that answer to no shared authority. Refineries and foundries that once ran as one network are strung across contested territory, their output seized and re-seized as fronts shift. Settlement remains moderate, most of it clustered around fortified works far from the ash-grey no-man's-land that scars the equatorial plants, and what wealth exists is guarded rather than shared. The civil war here is old enough that ruined districts are simply mapped around, not rebuilt.
226.inhabitants: The rodent population lives under a dictatorship that claims the whole world but controls only pieces of it, and most communities have learned to keep working regardless of which flag flies over the nearest checkpoint. Comfortable wealth persists in pockets loyal to whichever authority currently holds the industrial core, while those caught between factions get by on stockpiled goods and old machinery kept running past its intended service.

227.description: Qutiri's ancient mountain ranges, worn smooth by age, ring settlements built low and reinforced against the ground's frequent violence. Its industrial base, refineries, foundries, and processing yards, sprawls across the flatter basins where tremors do less damage to heavy plant, though the risk is never absent. Building codes here are strict and visible, with bracing and dampers worked into even modest structures, a response to the deadly earthquakes that periodically strike without much warning.
227.inhabitants: The competing local authorities that govern Qutiri rarely agree on much, but seismic building standards remain one of the few matters on which all factions cooperate without dispute. Colonials here tend toward practical, unsentimental attitudes, shaped by industrial routine and by a landscape that can, on short notice, take away what has been built.'

228.description: Biramabi presents flat, unremarkable farmland broken only by irrigation ditches and the low sheds where grain is stored before collection. Fields are worked in rotation under a collective schedule, with tools kept simple and machinery scarce. Settlements are few and spread thin across the plain, each little more than a cluster of dwellings around a granary and a meeting hall. Travelers and residents alike describe the place, without much argument, as dull.
228.inhabitants: The colonists work the land in assigned shifts under local commissars who see to quotas rather than comfort, and little is left over once the harvest is divided. Life follows the planting calendar closely, and conversation tends toward the weather and the yield rather than anything else. They are plain, steady people, unused to visitors and in no hurry to impress them.

229.description: Soorbi's continents are given over almost entirely to foundries, refineries and the tenement blocks that house their workers, laid out in the same grey grid pattern that state planners favoured across the settled districts generations ago. Smoke haze sits permanently over the lowlands, and rivers running past the smelting complexes carry a persistent metallic tint. Off-world references to the place are uniformly unflattering, and little on the surface argues against the reputation; it is a functional, thoroughly used-up world rather than a scenic one.
229.inhabitants: The population, fierce furry rodents organised under strict collective ownership of the mills and mines, take a grim pride in output quotas rather than surroundings. Wages and rations are steady enough to keep discontent low, and most regard complaints about the smog or the architecture as beside the point of the work itself.

230.description: Solageon's rivers and aquifers carry a toxin that has never been fully explained, so every farm and township depends on cisterns fed by filtration towers rather than the surface water that laces the lowlands. Its agricultural belts are worked in bands well back from the contaminated floodplains, where irrigation is drawn from treated reserves rather than the land's own supply. The forests beyond the farms shelter the tree wolf, a pack hunter whose reputation has spread well past this system and which keeps most clearing and logging confined to daylight hours. Administration is split among a patchwork of separate local governments, each holding its own stretch of cleared land and its own water-treatment charter.
230.inhabitants: Solageonian colonials are farmers first, raised from childhood to read the color of a stream before touching it and to keep dogs and fences between their herds and the tree line. Poverty and modest tooling make every filtration tower and irrigation channel a shared civic project, maintained through endless small negotiations between neighboring jurisdictions that answer to no common authority. It has made them practical, guarded people, more comfortable trusting a treaty with the next township than trusting the ground beneath their own fields.

231.description: Tiquat's cities rise in tight rings of foundries and refineries, their streets lined with the great parking meters for which the world is known, oversized iron sentinels that have become as much a symbol of the place as its industry. The ground beneath them is unreliable, and unpredictable earthquakes periodically level whole districts, forcing constant rebuilding in steel and reinforced ceramics. Advanced engineering keeps the factories running despite the tremors, with structures braced and re-braced against a landscape that never quite settles.
231.inhabitants: The population lives under a dictatorship that directs labour toward the factories with the same discipline it applies to quake recovery, and comfort here is earned through steady industrial output rather than leisure. Tiquat's colonials are practical, unsentimental people, accustomed to rebuilding what the ground takes from them and quick to return to work once the shaking stops.

232.description: Rexebe presents a continuous surface of manufacturing districts and residential towers, its skyline broken by corporate insignia rather than any natural feature. Beneath the industrial output, the world has cultivated a reputation far removed from its factories: its night districts run through every hour of the local clock, and its kitchens draw on ingredients shipped in from far-flung holdings to produce dishes found nowhere else. Advanced infrastructure keeps the crowded arcologies fed, lit and entertained without evident strain.
232.inhabitants: The Black Bony Humanoids who fill Rexebe's towers work under corporate charter, their labour, leisure and diet all managed by the same holding structures that own the land beneath them. Wealth here buys refinement rather than leisure alone, and locals speak of their chefs and club proprietors with the same pride others reserve for engineers.

233.description: Qubeen's foundries and refineries sit behind earthworks and stockade walls, testimony to a civil war that flares and subsides without pattern across the sizeable landmass. Great tracts of the world lie empty between the holdings of rival lords, whose smokestacks mark the only settlements worth the name. Machinery here is patched and repatched rather than replaced, the ironworks running on whatever coal and ore the current front allows through. Roads exist mostly as memory; supply moves under guard or not at all.
233.inhabitants: The colonials owe labor and loyalty to whichever lord holds their district this season, and switch allegiance as the fighting shifts the map beneath them. Life is measured in shifts at the furnace and turns at the wall, and few expect either arrangement to outlast the year.

234.description: Cetiisqu carries its industry in scattered foundries and refineries that answer to local lords rather than any central authority, their smoke drifting over fields worked in the old manner. The world is best known off-planet for the Cetiisquian evil Bioid, a construct whose reputation has long overtaken the modest workshops that first built its kind. Settlements sit apart from one another, each clustered around a keep or manor that owns the works nearby, and the roads between them are poorly kept.
234.inhabitants: People here answer first to their liege and only distantly to any wider notion of a government, and their labor in the foundries is bound up with old obligations of land and service. Life is plain and the work is hard, and most speak of the Bioid the way one speaks of a bad harvest that keeps returning.

235.description: Rebia's continents are given over almost entirely to collective farmland, wide floodplains and irrigated terraces that ring shallow, warm seas under a permanently damp sky. The world's size allows for vast, low-yield-per-hectare but enormous-in-aggregate grain and marsh-crop cooperatives, administered from clusters of concrete silos and dormitory blocks rather than true cities. Rebia is known throughout the region less for its harvests than for the peculiar reticence of its people, who are said to vanish from open ground the moment a stranger's shadow falls across the paddies.
235.inhabitants: The population is composed of frogs organized into work brigades under a rigidly egalitarian, state-planned system that prizes quiet diligence over ambition. Generations of collective labor have not made them gregarious; visitors to any given commune more often hear the workers than see them, since the moment attention turns their way they retreat into the reeds and canals. Even among themselves they are said to prefer written directives and shared silence to conversation, conducting the business of the harvest with a minimum of fuss and an almost total avoidance of eye contact.

236.description: Ordima is a wide, thinly peopled world of small holdings scattered across a poor and unforgiving countryside, where farming remains a matter of hand tools and stubborn animals rather than machinery. Villages sit far apart under overlapping and often contradictory local authorities, each with its own petty rules and tariffs. The one thing that unites them is a shared kitchen tradition: a goat soup, thick with root vegetables and unfamiliar spice, cooked differently in every district but claimed proudly by all.
236.inhabitants: The colonials here are goat-herders and root farmers first, subjects of whichever council or headman holds the nearest town second, and their loyalties rarely extend past the boundary of their own district. Generations of primitive tools and poor soil have made them patient, thrifty, and unhurried by outside notions of progress. Cooking, particularly of the soup that carries the world's name to other systems, is treated as a serious and competitive craft.

237.description: Aruszati's industrial belts ring its equator in continuous bands of foundries, refineries and orbital shipyards, feeding the arenas that have made the world synonymous with Zero-G cricket. The sport is played in vast rotating stadiums slung in high orbit, connected to the surface by tether lines that double as freight elevators for the factories below. Cities on the ground are laid out around these tether termini, dense and vertical, built to move workers and spectators alike with equal efficiency.
237.inhabitants: The population works long shifts in advanced industry and treats the orbital game as both civic pastime and export commodity, with league schedules debated as fiercely as parliamentary votes. Elected councils, answerable to a wealthy and heavily populated electorate, keep close ties between corporate output and public spectacle, so that factory shift patterns and match calendars are drawn up together.

238.description: Zaleriza turns slowly through unremarkable seasons, its farmland spread thin across scattered valleys with nothing to distinguish one field from the next. No central authority organizes the harvests or the roads, so cultivation follows old habit rather than plan, and settlements exist as loose clusters separated by long stretches of empty ground. Little of note has ever happened here, and the world's reputation for dullness is, if anything, earned by its unbroken sameness.
238.inhabitants: The Fierce Bony Lobsters that work this soil answer to no government beyond their own hard-shelled tempers, settling disputes over land and water without appeal to higher law. Poverty and primitive tools keep their days given over to plain labor, and what little excitement exists among them tends to come from each other rather than from the world around them.

239.description: Zasoer is a compact agricultural world whose farms lie scattered across a handful of fertile basins, worked with tools and methods that have changed little across generations. The short daylight hours are given to the fields, but once the sun goes down the townships along the basin edges light lanterns and open their squares, and it is this after-dark custom, part market and part festival, that travelers from farther worlds have come to remark upon. The settlements themselves remain small and loosely joined, each answering to its own local council under the wider confederate arrangement that binds the world together.
239.inhabitants: The colonials of Zasoer divide their lives cleanly between the labor of the day and the looser, freer hours after dusk, when farmers, traders and neighboring hamlets mix in ways the daylight economy does not allow. Governed by consensus rather than command, the confederacy's loose hold over daily affairs leaves each township to keep its own customs, and the nights have grown into something distinctly local and, by all report, worth staying up for.

240.description: Raleen's continents are given over almost entirely to manufacturing districts, refineries and the dense residential blocks needed to house the workforce that runs them. Between the industrial zones, plantations of native hardwood are cultivated less for timber than for the tree grub that burrows in its bark, a delicacy exported across the region and celebrated in festivals throughout the year. The confederated council districts that govern the planet are wealthy enough to keep the air scrubbed and the transit lines running, giving the world a curiously tidy look despite the scale of its industry.
240.inhabitants: Generations of steady prosperity under confederate rule have left the population secure enough to indulge a reputation for absurdity, and Raleenians treat eccentric humour, elaborate practical jokes and grub-eating contests as civic pastimes rather than embarrassments. Workers in the industrial districts take pride in their output during the day and their foolishness after hours, and visitors are often surprised how seriously the planet takes not being serious.

241.description: Qurave's industrial belts ring the equator in continuous grey districts, their advanced fabrication plants running on ore and feedstock that never quite matches demand. The poor yield of the world's own resources keeps the economy lean despite the sophistication of its machinery, and much of the population is packed into dense residential blocks built hard against the factory walls. Amid the smoke and structure, the terraced vineyards of the southern lowlands persist, producing the Quravian Ervesori brandy that carries the world's name beyond its own sky.
241.inhabitants: Life under the dictatorship is ordered and closely managed, with labour assignments and housing allotments handled by the same authority that oversees the factories. Comfortable wages soften the discipline, and workers speak of the vineyard shifts as a favoured posting, a season of cleaner air and better company away from the industrial districts.

242.description: Atrebibi is a small world of terraced farmland and irrigation canals, its close horizon giving the fields a folded, compressed look from any elevation.
