The land is given over almost entirely to agricultural leases held by the governing corporate boards, with grain silos and processing sheds marking the boundaries between company parcels. It is best known offworld for the Atrebibian deadly monkey, a native predator that farm cooperatives tolerate as pest control despite the periodic mauling reported in the outlying holdings. Settlements cluster tightly around the processing centers, laid out to company specification rather than any older civic plan.
242.inhabitants: The Slimy Frogs who work the terraces do so under contract to the boards that own the land beneath them, and their lives follow the harvest schedules set from the corporate offices. Comfortable wages and steady work have made them a settled, unhurried people, though most keep a healthy distance from the tall grass where the monkeys are known to hunt.

243.description: Broad continents of cultivated lowland give Teesdi its living, with grain belts and pasture running out toward horizons flattened by the world's size. Solar flare activity strikes the upper atmosphere on an irregular cycle, scorching crops and disrupting communications across whole farming districts before subsiding. Kitchens and smallholdings across the settled belt turn out the shrew cutlet the world is named for elsewhere in the charts, a dish tied closely to the rhythms of the harvest calendar. Towns are strung along the fertile river valleys, each with its own grain silos and market halls built to withstand the periodic disruption from above.
243.inhabitants: The population lives spread across farm cooperatives and market towns, governed by elected councils that answer directly to a populace used to voting on local matters. Comfortable but not idle, the colonials keep close watch on weather and sky alike, and treat the solar disruptions as an accepted cost of settling so large and open a world.

244.description: Ararus spreads wide beneath scattered clearings of pink Lasoteza tulips, their plantations cut into the edges of forests that grow with a tangled, almost feverish exuberance. No central authority has ever organized the world's use, so plots are worked and abandoned according to whoever holds them at the time, and the tulip fields blur into wild growth without clear boundary. Settlements are few and far between, thin clusters of dwellings set against a landscape that otherwise belongs to the forest.
244.inhabitants: The small rodents who work this soil answer to no government beyond custom and immediate need, tending tulip plots in loose, shifting arrangements that dissolve and reform with the seasons. Poverty and primitive tools keep ambitions modest, and life follows the rhythm of planting and forest foraging rather than any larger design.

245.description: Ara spreads across a broad landmass whose industry has long outstripped the will or means to maintain it, leaving smokestack towns half-abandoned between stretches of open, empty country. The disease that has taken hold here moves through the water and the wind alike, and entire districts are simply left to it, boarded up and unclaimed. What manufacturing continues does so in isolated pockets, run by whoever still has the strength and the machinery, with no central authority to say otherwise.
245.inhabitants: Without government, the colonials organize themselves in small, wary clusters, trading news of the sickness as carefully as they trade goods. Life here is shaped around avoidance and endurance, and those who have survived long tend to be self-reliant, close-mouthed, and slow to trust anyone claiming a cure.

246.description: Tianve's landmass is given over almost entirely to refining complexes, orbital component works, and the dense residential blocks built to house the workforce that runs them. Rivers here run through cooling channels before they run through anything natural, and the skyline is dominated by stack towers and gantry cranes rather than any older architecture. The world's fortunes rest on heavy manufacture sold across the trade lanes, and its cities have grown up around the factories rather than the other way round. Tianve is reasonably noted, if for anything beyond its output, for its people's peculiar and near-universal contempt for food blenders and for Zero-G cricket.
246.inhabitants: The population is dense, well paid, and organised into the unions and civic assemblies that keep an advanced industrial democracy running smoothly. Elections here are fought as fiercely over factory shift rules and housing allocation as over planetary policy, and most citizens hold strong, loudly aired opinions on matters both large and, apparently, kitchen-appliance-sized. Sport of the zero-gravity variety finds little affection among a people more inclined to argue about production quotas than fielding averages.

247.description: Quorte's farmland spreads across broad lowland basins beneath a sky that turns unpredictable during periods of heightened solar activity, when flare storms disrupt communications and scorch exposed crops. The corporate holdings that own most of the arable land have learned to time planting and harvest around these episodes, though losses are never fully avoidable. The Quortian tree wolf, native to the forested highlands beyond the farm belt, draws naturalists and hunters alike and remains the world's most recognized export in reputation if not in volume. Settlements cluster along river valleys where soil is richest and flare damage least severe.
247.inhabitants: The Black Rodents who work Quorte's fields and processing stations do so under contracts issued by the agricultural combines that govern the world, their days shaped as much by planting schedules as by solar forecasts. Generations of dealing with both corporate oversight and unpredictable skies have made them practical and unsentimental, quick to adapt plans and slow to complain about conditions beyond anyone's control.

248.description: Soladies turns broad river valleys and terraced hillsides into orchard and vineyard country, its modest holdings strung along the water in a pattern easy to see from the air. The distilleries that produce the fabled Soladiesian evil brandy sit close to the fields that feed them, walled compounds of copper stills and aging cellars cut into the hillside rock. Beyond the cultivated belts the land turns to scrub and stone, largely empty but for the roads that carry the harvest inward toward the capital.
248.inhabitants: Farming families and distillery hands make up most of the population, working land and stills under quotas set from the capital and enforced with little patience for argument. Life is steady rather than easy, and what pride the colonials take is reserved almost entirely for the brandy that carries the world's name beyond its own sky.

249.description: Maxeedso is a sizeable world given over almost entirely to rain forest, its canopy broken only by the terraced clearings where the confederated farm-holds grow their export crops. The climate is warm and wet through every season, feeding root and fruit yields that support settlements strung along river valleys rather than any single capital. The world is mildly known beyond its own region for the depth of these forests and for the tree wolf, a canopy predator whose range spans the wetter provinces. Modest workshops process timber and produce at the edges of the holds, but the forest itself is left largely uncut by agreement among the member-states.
249.inhabitants: The small black fat insects that farm and govern Maxeedso organize themselves into loose confederated holds, each self-sufficient in food and jealous of its say in shared decisions. Comfortable but unhurried, they measure standing in granaries filled and forest left standing rather than in goods sold outward, and they speak of the tree wolf with the wary respect due a neighbor rather than a curiosity.

250.description: Xexedi is a small world whose industrial capacity far outstrips its modest surface area, its foundries and refineries stacked into vertical districts to spare land for housing. Advanced sanitation systems ring every settlement, a costly necessity rather than a civic luxury, for the planet remains scourged by a disease that resists all attempts at eradication. Wealth here is measured against constant medical expenditure, and the skyline is dominated as much by quarantine towers as by manufacturing spires.
250.inhabitants: The population lives under a confederacy of member-districts that pool their considerable industrial wealth to fund research and containment rather than expansion. Colonial by descent and pragmatic by necessity, the people work in sealed factories and filtered streets, treating rigorous health discipline as simply the price of staying rich and staying alive.

251.description: Xexeti is a small volcanic world where thin bands of ash-fed soil support the terraced plots scattered between fields of cooled lava. The great cones that dominate the horizon vent steadily, and settlement clusters low and cautious on their older, quieter slopes. Farming here is a matter of watching the sky for smoke rather than rain, and the fields are worked with tools that owe nothing to any factory. The planet's edible arts graduates, trained in small kitchens rather than institutions, are locally celebrated for turning the poor harvests into something worth talking about.
251.inhabitants: Without any central authority to organize them, the colonials rely on kinship and old habit to divide land, water and volcanic warning duties among themselves. Life is hard and the margins thin, but a stubborn pride attaches to the cooking of a poor harvest well, and the title of edible arts graduate is earned rather than granted.

252.description: Tiinlebi's arable land clings to terraced valleys between long ranges of weathered stone, where thin soil and short growing seasons keep the farms modest and the harvests uneven. The Tiinlebian mountain slug, gathered from damp slopes above the terraces, is the one export that carries the world's name beyond its own sky. Villages are built low and close along the valley floors, connected by cart roads rather than anything faster, in keeping with a colony that never industrialized its kitchens or much else.
252.inhabitants: Farmers here vote on grain quotas and water rights with the same seriousness they bring to slug harvests, the democracy running mostly through town meetings and shared ledgers rather than any distant capital. Meals are prepared by hand, chopped and pounded rather than machined, and the settlers speak of food blenders with a stubborn, almost inherited contempt that outsiders rarely understand and locals rarely bother explaining.

253.description: Rateedar's industrial belts run in broken lines across its temperate lowlands, each stretch of foundries and refineries claimed by a different local authority. No single government controls the world, and the resulting patchwork of rival administrations has hardened into open civil war, with factory towns changing hands and production lines switching allegiance as often as territory does. Advanced fabrication plants keep running through the fighting, their output diverted according to whichever faction holds the surrounding district in a given season.
253.inhabitants: The population is a comfortable, populous mass of harmless insectoid natives, organized into competing regional governments rather than any unified state. Each faction maintains its own workers, administrators and militias, and loyalty tends to follow hive-district and factory rather than any broader notion of nationhood.

254.description: Solar flares scour Onlema's upper atmosphere on a near-constant cycle, bathing the industrial belts in shifting auroral light and forcing power grids to run on redundant, radiation-hardened relays. The world's factories and refineries sprawl across shielded lowland basins, their domed roofs and buried conduits built specifically to survive the storms overhead. Wealth here comes from heavy manufacturing rather than agriculture, with entire districts given over to smelting, alloy work, and the assembly of components too delicate to build under an open, unstable sky.
254.inhabitants: The population lives and works under centrally planned quotas, with labor collectives assigned to shifts timed around solar forecasts rather than any natural day. Generations of coping with the flares have made the workforce methodical and unsentimental, valuing reliable shielding and steady output over any comfort the surface might otherwise offer.

255.description: Orerve turns industrial output at a modest pace, its scattered works strung across a wide, thinly settled land rather than gathered into anything resembling a city. There is little to mark one district from the next: the same grey sheds, the same slow rhythm of shifts, the same flat horizon repeated across a sizeable world. Nothing here has ever drawn much notice, and the planet seems content to stay that way.
255.inhabitants: Local lords hold their scattered works under old feudal claim, and most people spend their working lives within sight of the estate that employs them. Wealth is modest and evenly thin, and the mood among the workforce is one of quiet, unremarkable endurance rather than complaint. Even the native rodents, harmless and unbothered, seem suited to a world that asks little and offers less.
